case_source:
(From judgment and order dated 25.7.74 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 
Khulna, in Miscellaneous Case No. 282 of 1972).
full_judgment:
A. M. Mahmudur Rahman, J.: This Miscellaneous Appeal is against the Judgment and order dated July, 25,1974 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Khulna, dismissing the Miscellaneous Case No. 282 of 1972 instituted upon an application under Or. 9 R.13 C.P.C. 

2. The Respondent 1 Instituted Money Suit No. 109 of 1970 against the Appellant. The suit was decreed ex-parte on July 14, 1972. Thereupon the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case was started. The learned Judge, on contest, dismissed the Miscellaneous Case leading to filing the present Miscellaneous Appeal. 

3. Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed seriously contends that the remark of the learned Judge on the demenanour of P.W.1 that the petitioner P.W. 1 at the time of this deposition was Speaking in a manner as if he was suppressing the real truth "under Or. 18 R.12 C.P.C. is not objective. He submits that the Court has power to make observation about the demeanour of a witness but such observation must not be subjective but must be based on objective materials. According to him, the observation is not based, in the instant case, on material object or in otherwise the observation is not objective but subjective. In support of his contention, he relied upon the decision in the case of Pothan Chandy Vs. Ouseph Kochousepth reported in A.I.R. 1951, Tri-Cochin 12. Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed referred me to paragraph 3 of the Judgment. The observation made at paragraph 3 of the decision relied upon by Mr. Ahmed does not support the contention of Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed. In the instant case the remark was made in the Judgment itself and not after closing the evidence and after reading over the same and signed by the Judge. In the aforesaid case, the application arose out of an application under Section 24 C.P.C. on the ground that the Judge after signing the deposition remarked this witness strike me as unscrupulous." In that Judgment the remark was made by the learned Judge after signing the deposition sheet unlike the present one where the remark was made in the body of the Judgment. Or. 18. R. 12 C.P.C. does not disentitled a Judge to make a remark on the demeanour of witness in the Judgment as has been done here. Therefore, on facts of this case, the principle laid down in Pothan Chandy has little application to the facts of the instant case. The decision does not help Mr. Shahabuddin as the remark was made in that case after closing the evidence and not in the body of the Judgment. The Court is not permitted to make remark about the demeanour of a witness after examination of the witness and after the deposition was read over and signed, but premises a Judge to make such remark in the body of the Judgment under Or. 18. r. 12. C.P.C. 

4. Now, let us see on merit, how far the Appellant was successful to prove his case. In other words, whether he was prevented from sufficient cause in not appearing at the time of hearing of the suit. On a careful perusal of the Judgment and order impugned, it appears that the learned Judge, after consideration of the evidence on record, came to the finding that the Petitioner willfully avoided to appear. This finding is based on the statement of the Petitioner himself who stated that he came to know about the ex-parte decree from one of the staffs of the Bank on 7.8.72, but he could not disclose the same to the employee when he was given such information. The learned Judge also noted material discrepancy in the statement of P.W.1 (Plaintiff) and his brother P.W.2 so far as handing over the papers and the power to the learned Advocate Mr. Delwar Hossain is concerned. It appears that the Petitioner stated in the petition under Or. 9 r. 13 C.P.C. that he handed over the power to Mr. Delwar Hossain, Advocate, without mentioning the year. He has also stated that he sent the papers through Biman from Dhaka. It is not understood how and why he handed over the power to Mr. Delwar Hossain through his brother when he sent the same through Biman. This contradiction was taken into consideration by the Court of Appeal in disbelieving the statement of P.W.1. In this regard Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed submits that during those troubled days, the power was sent per Avon to Mr. Delwar Hossain, but he was not at Khulna at that time and till 1973. He submits pointing to this aspect that the Court should take a lenient view to set aside an ex-parte decree which resulted from no laches or fault of the Advocate of the litigant. Thus, Court sometimes takes such view, but each case is to be decided on its peculiar facts and circumstances. In this case, in view of the findings of the Court, I am of the opinion that the findings are based on cogent reason on evidence and the learned Judge rightly arrived at a finding that the Appellant willfully avoided to appear when the suit was taken up for hearing. The Judgment impugned does not call for any interference. 

5. Accordingly, I affirm the Judgment, of the Courts below and the appeal is dismissed. No order as to costs. 

End.

full_judgment:
Amin-Ur-Rahman Khan J:—This Rule at the instance of the pre-emptee-petitioner is directed against the judgment and order of the Additional District-Judge, Rajshahi, in Misc. Appeal No. 32 of 1970 affirming the judgment and order of the Munsif, Nawabganj in Misc. Case N. 92 of 1968 allowing pre-emption in favour of the opposite party under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

2. The opposite party No. 1 being the petitioner brought Misc. Case No. 92 of 1968 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act seeking pre-emption of the land sold to the present petitioner upon the allegations that he was a co-sharer tenant by inheritance in the case holding and that the purchaser was a stranger and that no notice was served and the petitioner was not aware of the sale until 3.2.68.

3. The present petitioner being the opposite party resisted the application on the ground that the petitioner was aware of the sale as early as in April, 1967 from a salish attended by him over the sale and the application was consequently barred by limitation. It was also pleaded that some co-sharer tenants by inheritance were not impleaded and lastly that the O.P. purchaser had made improvement in the land after purchase.

4. Both the courts below found that the petitioner being a non-notified co-sharer and having no knowledge of the sale before 3.2.68 the application was in time and that there was no defect of parties nor there was any improvement made on the land and accordingly allowed the pre-emption.

5. The pre-emptee petitioner being aggrieved by the decrees of the courts below has obtained this rule.

6. Mr. Mokhtar Hossain, the learned Advocate for the petitioner frankly conceded that he does not press the objections on the point of limitation and on the point of improvement.

7. Mr. Mokhtar Hossain submitted that according to the judgments of both the courts below there were some co-sharer tenants by inheritance in respect of the case holding who were not made parties and that the courts below committed an error of law in holding that even in the absence of those persons there was no defect of parties and also that they committed error of law is allowing the pre-emption in the absence of the necessary parties.

8. Mr. Mokhtar Hossain stressed that according to subsection 2 of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act all co-sharers by inheritance were required to be made parties while seeking pre-emption by another co-sharer tenant by inheritance and that this being a mandatory requirement of law the omission to make the parties made the pre-emption case liable to be dismissed.

9. On the other hand, Mr. Akram Hossain Amin, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties contended that the adding of all co-sharer tenants as parties was merely a directory provision of law and that omission of such person could not make the case liable to be dismissed.

10. In this case it was found by the learned Munsif that the brothers of Rezia or their heirs never claimed any interest in the case land nor took any steps to have their names recorded and also lived far away. He however was of the opinion that only the recorded co-sharer tenants and those who asserted their right in the tenancy should be made parties to enable them to claim pre-emption. The learned Additional District Judge concurred with the said findings. Thus from the findings of both the courts below it Could be seen that there were some co-sharer tenants by inheritance in the holding who were not made parties in the pre-emption case. But the courts below gave a wrong finding that even though they were co-sharer tenants by inheritance they were not necessary parties because they did not have their names recorded and did not claim interest in the case land having lived far away. The law enjoins that in an application made by co-sharer tenant all other co-sharer tenants of the holding shall be made parties. In this case it has been concurrently found by the courts below that some of the co-sharer tenants by inheritance were not made parties. Now the question is whether for the omission in making the left out co-sharer tenants parties in the case, the case shall fill on that account or not. In other words whether the making of all the co-sharer tenants by inheritance parties in the case is mandatory or directory.

11. Mr. Akram Hossain Amin, in support of his contention that it was a directory provision of law and not a mandatory one referred to the decision of the case of Matilal Sikdar and others Vs. Benodini reported in 28 DLR (AD) (1976) page 5 wherein it has been held by the Appellate Division after over ruling the decision of a single Bench reported in 21 DLR page 262 that a suit cannot be defeated by reason of mis-joinder or non-joinder of parties and also that objection as to non-joinder or mis-joinder of parties must be taken at the earliest opportunity. The reasons for the aforesaid finding as was given by the Appellate Division was that unless objections on the ground of non-joinder of the parties are taken at the earliest possible opportunity such objections shall be deemed to have been waived. It 'may be noted that in that case before the Appellate Division the objection as to non-joinder of parties was taken only before the High Court Division and was not taken before the original court or the lower appellate Court. But in the case be before me the misc. case was filed on 27.3.68 and objection was filed on 20-6-68 noting objection as to defect of parties and also a petition was filed on 31.8.68 specifically giving the names and address of the co-sharer tenants who were necessary parties as co-sharer tenants and were not impleaded. The case was heard nearly 2 years after in 1970 by the trial court. So in the case before in there is no scope to say that there was any waiver on the side of the present petitioner in respect of their objection as to omission of necessary parties. This certainly distinguished the present case from the case of Matilal SikderVs. Benodini Dashi.

<u>12. Mr. Mokhtar Hossain referred to the decision in the case of Abdus Samad Vs. Sohrab Ali reported in 33 DLR Appellate Division, page 113 which was a later decision of the Appealable In this decision the earlier decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Matilal Sikdar Vs. Benodini Dashi was considered and according to this decision impleading of persons who are necessary parties to a pre-emption application is mandatory according to sub section 2 of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and it is not controlled by Order I Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It has also been held in this decision that plea of non-joinder of necessary parties should be taken before the trial and if the party seeking pre-emption fails to implead such a party whose existence is disclosed the right of pre-emption is lost. It has also been held that a co-sharer in the holding cannot be allowed to purchase the entire land without impleading the other co-sharers and thereby depriving them from getting share.</u>

<u>13. It may also be noted that according to sub section 4 of section 96 of the state Acquisition and Tenancy Act upon an application for pre-emption by one co-sharer, other co-sharers having notice of the application have a legal right to apply to join in the same application and to have rate able pre-emption. So this provision of law will be frustrated if some co-sharers are not made parties in the pre-emption case. From this also it must be held that making of all the co-sharers parties in the case for pre-emption is mandatory.</u>

14. Thus following the latest decision in the case of Abdus Samad Vs. Sohrab Ali it must be held that the present case for pre-emption must fail for not making some of the inherited co-sharers parties inspite of objection as to the defect of parties long before the hearing of the Case.

15. Consequently the judgment and decree passed by the courts below suffer from error of law and wrong exercise of jurisdiction.

16. The rule is accordingly made absolute. The judgment and decree passed by the courts below in respect of Misc. Case No. 92 of 1968 are set aside and the said Misc. case is dismissed.

End.

case_source: Arising out of an application under Order 21 Rule 35 C.P.C.
full_judgment:
Bimalendu Bikash Roy Chowdhury, J: This Rule raises a short but subtle question as to the scope of Order 21 Rule 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The question arises in the following circumstances:

On 2nd February, 1977 petitioner No.1 Ahmed Ali along-with one Forman Gani, predecessor-in-interest of petitioner No. 2 Suna Ban and one Mariam Begum obtained an exparte decree against opposite party No. 1, Monsur Rahman and are Ambar Ali, husband of opposite party No. 2 Meher Negar and others in the following terms:

"That the suit the decreed exparte with costs. The right title and interest of the plaintiff over the suit land be decreed and they do get khas possession in respect of the same by evicting the defendants therefrom and removing all obstacles. The defendants are however, permitted to remove their structures upon suit land within 30 days of the decree failing which the plaintiffs will be at liberty to get the structures removed by putting the decree into execution."

2. The defendants preferred an application under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code to have the decree set aside but lost. They took an appeal therefrom. While the appeal was pending the decree holders levied an execution case and a writ for delivery of possession was issued. On a prayer made by the judgment-debtors the appellate court passed an order staying further proceedings of the execution case till the disposal of the appeal. The executing court accordingly recalled the writ and stayed all further proceedings of the execution. The appeal ended in dismissal on 17th March, 1979. Sometime in May, 1979 the decree holders levied a second execution case and a fresh writ under Order 21 Rule 35 of the Code was issued on 22nd May, 1979 directing the plaintiff to deliver possession to the decree holders and authorising him to remove any person bound by the decree who might refuse to vacate. Before the returnable date an application was made by the decree-holders seeking dismissal of the previous execution case on the ground that through oversight the subsequent execution case was started. On receipt thereof the court passed an order recalling the writ and directed that the application be heard in presence of the learned Advocates of the parties. The application eventually came up for consideration on 4th July, 1979 when the court made an order striking off the subsequent execution case on the view that during the pendency of one execution case for the same decree, there could not be another fresh execution case which was of course, not consonant to the settled principle that several execution cases may be in progress at one and the same time (Ref: Sarasti Prasad Vs. People's Industrial Bank Ltd. AIR 1917 Allahabad 129, Makhan Lal V. Mr. Bhagwana Kuer AIR 1936, Allahabad 655, Morarjee Gokuldas & CO. V. Sholapur Spinning and Weaving Co. Ltd. & others, AIR 1941 Born. 37 and Om Prakash V. Sm. Tahera Begum & ors. AIR 1955 Allahabad 382). The order, however, was not challenged from any side. As a result only the previous execution case remained pending.

3. In the meantime the peon who was directed to execute the decree submitted his report to the effect that the agent of the decree holders had been delivered possession on 30th May 1979 by fixing bamboo pegs after beating of drum. There was no indication in the report that the peon gave possession of the decretal land to the decree holders after evicting the judgment-debtors and removing all obstacles and structures therefrom as provided in the decree. As a matter of fact, it is not, disputed by the opposite parties that actual delivery of possession was not obtained by the decree-holders.

4. In the circumstances as the decree-holders pressed for fresh execution the judgment-debtors filed an objection under section 47 of the Code on the plea that the decree having once been executed, the same could not be executed again. It was resisted by the decree-holders saying that actual delivery of possession having not been made in terms of the decree, they were entitled to obtain actual possession of the decretal land on the footing of the decree.

5. The executing court over-ruled the objection of the judgment-debtors but on appeal the decision was reversed and the objection upheld. Being aggrieved the decree-holders have preferred this revisional application.

6. On behalf of the petitioners it is urged by Mr. Fazlul Karim the learned Advocate that the decree sought to be executed being one for khas possession by evicting the judgment-debtors from the decretal land after removing all obstacles and structures standing thereon, it was the duty of the court to execute the same in terms thereof and in the manner provided by Order 21 Rule 35 of the Code according to which the actual possession or the land ought to have been delivered to the decree-holders and since the decree-holders had been delivered symbolical possession instead of actual possession to which they were entitled under the decree, it is not only proper but incumbent for the court to order for fresh delivery of possession in the facts of the case. The learned Advocate, therefore, maintains that the court of appeal below committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in dismissing the execution case as being not maintainable.

7. In reply Mr. S. R. Pal, the learned Advocate who appears for the judgment-debtors-opposite-parties contends that the decree-holders accepted delivery of symbolical possession without removal of the persons in possession and of the structures standing on the decretal land and so they cannot now proceed with the execution for khas possession. According to him the decree-holders by their own conduct have disentitled themselves to the remedy they now ask for and the only remedy now lying open to them is to go for a suit.

8. There being no ruling of this court on the point, several decisions from the Indian jurisdiction have been cited in support of the respective submissions of the learned Advocate.

One such case is Abdul Humid Vs. Prakash Chandra Nandi & others, AIR 1934 Cal. 793. In that case the decree-holders in a suit for partition were delivered possession in execution of the final decree, but it was found that they actually did not get possession of their shares, as some huts belonging to other co-sharer were standing thereon. The decree holders, therefore, applied for fresh delivery of possession by removal of the huts. The judgment-debtor raised an objection under section 47 of the Code. The executing court over ruled the objection and passed an order for delivery of possession by removing the huts. The judgment-debtor then preferred an appeal to the Calcutta High Court. It was argued before it that the executing court by ordering for fresh execution acted beyond jurisdiction. Division Bench of the said court comprising Lort Williams and M.C. Ghose, JJ answered the question in the following words:

"The first ground taken in appeal is that the court below acted without jurisdiction inasmuch as there is no provision in law for a second delivery of possession. It appears that the delivery of possession made on 24th April 1932 was not complete. Under the final decree the respondents were entitled to get actual possession and as the appellant had some huts standing on a portion of the land they could not get actual possession. In the circumstances, the court acted within jurisdiction in ordering a fresh delivery of possession by removing the huts of the appellant."

9. The same view appears to have been followed in Ghanshyam Das Mour Agarwalla Vs. Fatik Chandra Das, AIR 1957 Assam 123. In that case the decree-holder obtained a decree for delivery of possession and compensation. He levied execution of the decree. In execution of the writ for possession, the Nazir purported to give delivery of possession to the decree-holder and submitted a report to that effect. Accordingly, the court recorded an order saying that possession had been delivered and dismissed the execution case. The decree-holder thereafter took out a fresh execution of the decree. The judgment-debtor filed an objection to the execution. One of his contentions was that a second execution case could not be started in view of the report of the Nazir. The executing court rejected the objection and directed delivery of possession to be given to the decree-holder, but on appeal the order was set aside. The decree-holder then preferred an appeal to the Assam High Court. A Division Bench of that court allowed the appeal and set aside the order appealed against. In course of the judgment Sarjoo Prosad, C.J. speaking for the court observed.

"If the fact is, as it has been found in this case and not disputed by the respondent, that actual delivery of possession was not obtained by the decree-holder in the previous execution case, we see no justification for holding that the decree-holder should be deprived of his right to come before the executing Court and pray for a fresh delivery of possession, when there was no other bar to his right of executing the decree."

10. Similar view has also been expressed in Kaku Singh and others Vs. Gobind Singh and others, AIR 1959 Punjab 468. In that case a Single Bench comprising A.N. Grover, J. observed:

"It seems to me when after obtaining symbolical possession the decree-holder applies for delivery of actual possession, the execution proceeding either continues or starts afresh, because when formal possession has been given in execution proceedings a fresh application in execution for actual possession of the property can be maintained and such proceedings will clearly be execution proceedings. There is no need to bring a suit for recovery of actual possession even if symbolical possession had previously been delivered and actual possession can be obtained by means of execution."

In Shew Bux Mohata and another Vs. Bengal Breweries Ltd. and others AIR 1961 S.C. 137 cited by Mr. Pal, however, it is laid down that where the decree-holders of their own accepted delivery of possession with the judgment debtor remaining on the premises with their permission and they granted a receipt acknowledging full delivery of possession and put their guards on the premises and further permitted the execution case to be dismissed on the basis that full possession had been delivered to them by defendant, they are bound to the position that the decree has been fully executed and the decree cannot be executed any more. Their Lordships of Supreme Court of India referred with approval to a Calcutta case Viz. Jagadish Nath Roy Vs. Nafar Chandra Pramanik AIR 1931 Cal. 427=35 C.W.N. 12 for the view.

11. In the said Calcutta case, in execution of a decree for khas possession after demolition of the structure a writ under Order 21 Rule 35 of the Code was issued. The peon delivered possession to the agent of the decree-holder by fixing up a bamboo accompanied with beating of drum. On the returnable date the decree-holder appeared in the court to put in talabana for issue of notice as regards the execution of the decree for costs, but raised no objection of his not having khas possession in accordance with the terms of the writ and the court recorded an order "possession delivered on the decretal land". Subsequently the decree-holder made second application for execution praying khas possession. A question, therefore, arose whether a fresh execution was permissible in the said circumstances. The question was answered in the negative. Mukerjee, J. who delivered the judgment for a Division Bench expressed himself in the following language:"

The case, therefore, seems to me be one of those cases in which a decree-holder having armed himself with a decree for khas possession executes that decree in the first instance by obtaining symbolical possession only with some ulterior object of his own and thereafter subsequently and as a second installment asks for khas possession. The question is whether such a course is permissible under the law. I am of opinion that it is not."

12. In none of these two decisions the correctness of the view expressed in Abdul Hamid vs. Prakash Chandra Nandi and others (Supra) was yen doubted, rather it was expressly recognised in AIR 1931 Cal. 427 when the learned Judge said:

"If in the present case the conduct of the decree-holder might be construed as indicating a repudiation on his part of the symbolical possession which the peon had given him or at least as disclosing desire on his part not to be content at the time with the kind of possession that the peon had given him but to get the khas possession which he was entitled to under the decree and for which he had prayed in his first application for execution, I should be prepared to hold that he was perfectly within his rights to come before the executing Court to have his remedy."

<u>13. Turning now to the merit of the case before me, it appears that excepting a receipt of the agent of the decree-holders acknowledging that he had received delivery of possession of the kind mentioned in the peon's report no other material suggestive of the decree holder's acquiescence could be brought to the notice of this court. The receipt may "be read as merely reciting what the peon had done" as pointed out in the case reported in AIR 1931 Cal. 427. In the circumstances I am unable to draw any conclusion that the symbolical possession was the only kind of possession that the decree-holders wanted to have. The present case is thus distinguishable from the facts of the case reported in AIR 1931 Cal. 427 and AIR 1961 (S.C) 137 and hence the principle enunciated in those cases are in applicable to this case.</u>

<u>14. There being no bar to the right of the decree-holders to get the actual possession of the property in terms of the decree and the policy of law being to avoid multiplicity of the proceedings I find no reason why they should be driven to a suit. I, therefore, hold that the court of appeal below committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned order.</u>

<u>I accordingly, make the rule absolute, set aside impugned order and restore that of the executing Court.</u>

<u>I, therefore, make no order as to costs.</u>

End.

full_judgment:
Md Emdadul Huq J: This Civil Revision has arisen from Title Suit No. 59 of 1986. In that suit, the learned Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Sadar, Comilla, by judgment and order dated 28-2-1987, allowed to the petitioner-plaintiff a decree of permanent injunction in respect of some land; but, in Title Appeal No. 118 of 1987, the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Comilla, by his judgment and order dated 28-4-1998, reversed the decision of the trial court and thereby dismissed the said suit.

2. The Rule issued in this Revision was earlier disposed of by another Single Bench of this Court by judgment dated 30-8-2010. But, in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal (CPLA) No. 113 of 2010, the Appellate Division has sent this Revision on remand for fresh hearing and disposal by this Bench with some observations and direction as quoted in the findings and decision portion of this judgment.

3. Accordingly the matter has been heard afresh in presence of the learned Advocates for both sides. For convenient disposal of the Rule, the relevant aspects of the matter are presented below under proper headings.

Plaintiffs' Case.

4. Petitioner Md Wahid Miah, as plaintiff No. 1 and his paternal uncle's wife (DO) Rajaban Nesa, as plaintiff No. 2, filed the above noted suit for permanent injunction for protection of their possession over the suit land measuring 5 decimals.

5. During pendency of the suit, plaintiff No. 2 Rajaban Nessa died without leaving any heir. Her name was deleted by the trial court by order dated 13-1-1987 and plaintiff No. 1 (petitioner) was substituted as her successor-in-interest on the basis of a claim that she had made an oral gift of the suit land to plaintiff No. 1. Plaintiff claims that the suit land is part of CS Plot No. 161 measuring 19 decimals appertaining to CS Khatian No. 23. The land of this khatian and that of No. 37 belonged to CS recorded tenant Mon Gazi who had orally gifted the suit plot No. 161 to his two domestic servants in two portions, namely 12 decimals to Golam Ali and 7 decimals to Nowab Ali.

6. The said 7 decimals of Nawab Ali was inherited by his son Yakub Ali who sold the same to one Hafizuddin. Deceased plaintiff No. 2 Rajaban Nessa had purchased the suit land from the said Hafizuddin by a registered kabala dated 20-2-1954 and had been in possession thereof.

7. Plaintiff No. 2 was a childless old lady. So plaintiff No.1 as the nearest relative, used to take care of her. Before her death she orally gifted the suit land to plaintiff No. 1. Thus plaintiff No. 1 acquired the suit land and has been in possession.

8. The remaining property of Mon Gazi devolved upon his only son Hari Dhon and, on his death, upon his three daughters including defendant Nos. 3 and 4 Amena and Abeda. These grand-daughters of Mon Gazi had sold 68 decimals to one Tamiz Uddin and 32 decimals to his brother Sayed Ali, both being residents of the suit village and they have been possessing the same.

9. The grand-daughters of Mon Gazi were given in marriage with residents of different villages. So they used to look after their remaining property through one Abdus Salam of the suit village. This Abdus Salam, at one stage, threatened plaintiffs' possession over the suit land. So the plaintiff got a registered a Nadabi Deed dated 27-8-1982 executed by the said Amena and Abeda, the two grand-daughters of Mon Gazi. In this deed they have admitted the fact of oral gift of the suit plot 50 years back by their grand-father Mon Gazi to the two domestic servants and they have further stated that they do not claim the suit land.

10. Defendant No. 1, Abdul Khaleque, being grandson of the said Nowab Ali, with the assistance of defendant No.2 Abdul Khaleque son of Abdur Rahman, threatened plaintiffs' possession on 16-9-1982 on the basis of some forged documents showing a false certificate case and auction sale therein. Hence, the suit.

Defendant's Case:

11. The opposite party-defendant No. 1, Abdul Khaleque son of Yakub Ali, in his written statement denies plaintiffs' title and possession and the alleged threat to their possession. However he admits that Mon Gazi was the original owner of the suit khatian No. 23 including the suit land and non-suit khatian No. 37 and that Mongazi had a son named Hari Dhon. But Hari Dhon died during the life time of Mon Gazi. So Hari Dhon and his daughters did not inherit anything from Mon Gazi, rather the surviving three daughters of Mon Gazi, being Arafaner Nesa and two others inherited the interest of Mon Gazi.

Defendant further claims that, due to arrears of rent, Certificate Case No. 1227 of 1952-53 was initiated against the said daughters of Mon Gazi and others in respect of the properties left by Mon Gazi. In this case, one Salamat Ullah and 5 others auction purchased the entire land of CS khatian Nos. 23 and 37 and got delivery of possession thereof. The SA khatian No. 44 has accordingly been prepared in the names of the auction purchasers in respect of the land of CS khatian No. 23 and they paid rent to Government.

12. There was an amicable partition among the auction purchasers and the suit plot No. 161 fell in the share of auction purchaser Salamat Ullah from whom defendant No. 1, by registered kabala dated 20-7-1981, purchased the suit land and has been in possession thereof.

13. Defendant No. 2, Abdul Khaleque son of Abdur Rahman has also purchased 7 decimals of the suit plot by a registered kabala dated 20-7-1981 from another auction purchaser named Idris Miah and defendant No. 2 has been in possession thereof.

Deliberation in the Revision.

14. At the hearing of this Revision, Mr Md Abul Kalam Patwary, the learned Advocate for the petitioner (plaintiff), submits that the appellate court committed an error of law in holding that the vendor of defendant No. 1 had acquired title and possession on the basis of the auction sale in a certificate case initiated in 1952-53, because, at that time, the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (shortly the Act, 1950) was not in force and that this Act came into the force in April, 1956 in Comilla district and therefore the Certificate Officer had no legal authority to initiate that case or to transfer the land by auction sale.

15. Mr Patwary, the learned Advocate, next submits that prima facie title and exclusive possession of the plaintiff has been proved by the local witnesses, who clearly stated the fact of possession of Nowab Ali the domestic servant of Mon Gazi and also by the Nadabi Deed executed by the grand daughters of Mon Gazi admitting the oral gift made by their grandfather Mon Gazi to Nowab Ali and Golam Ali and by the document of purchase of deceased plaintiff Rajaban Nessa from the successor-in-interest of Nowab Ali and lastly by the oral gift by deceased plaintiff Rajaban Nessa to plaintiff No. 1. In reply, Mr Abdul Kuddus Miah, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite party, submits that, irrespective of the weakness of the defendant's evidence, the plaintiff must prove his own case, but he has totally failed to prove his prima facie title, as he was a mere care taker and not even an heir of the other plaintiff being deceased Rajaban Nessa, and also failed to prove his exclusive possession.

16. Mr Kuddus Mia, the learned Advocate, next submits that neither the oral gift allegedly made by Mon Gazi in favour the two domestic servants, Nowab Ali and Golam Ali, nor the oral gift allegedly made by deceased plaintiff Rajaban Nessa to plaintiff No.1 was proved to be any credible testimony. Mr Kuddus Mia, the learned Advocate, next submits that the Nadabi Deed executed by the daughters of Hari Dhon does not help establish plaintiffs title, as the executants themselves had no title, because of the alleged oral gift by Mon Gazi to Nowab Ali and the auction sale held in the certificate case.

17. Mr Kuddus Mia, the learned Advocate, next submits that the documents of auction purchase (Exhibits-B, C and D) remain valid until those are set aside in a proper legal proceedings, that the auction purchase has been reflected in the SA Khatian (Exhibit-E) prepared in the names of the auction purchasers and that this khatian is to be presumed as correct unless rebutted by better evidence and the khatian read with the rent receipts (Exhibit-F, F(1) and F(2)) and the oral evidence of the DW's sufficiently prove possession of the defendant.

Findings and decision in Revision

18. Principal controversies: The only fact admitted by both sides is that the entire holding of CS khatian No. 23 including suit plot No. 161 belonged to CS tenant Mon Gazi.

19. The parties differ on the two fundamental questions of facts namely:- (1) whether Mon Gazi orally gifted the suit land to his domestic servant Nowab Ali, and whether this gift ultimately led to acquisition of the suit land by the plaintiff, and (2) whether the interest of the successors-in-interest Mon Gazi extinguished because of a Certificate Case initiated in 1952-53 due to arrear of rent, and whether the auction sale therein led to acquisition of the suit land by the defendant.

20. The principal legal issue is whether the Certificate Officer had the lawful authority to initiate the certificate case and to transfer the suit land by the alleged auction sale.

21. Opposite decision of the Courts below:

The trial court, upon discussion of the evidence on record believed the case of the plaintiff and decreed the suit. But the appellate court upon independent assessment of the evidence on record reversed the decision of the trial court and dismissed the suit. The appellate court, however, recorded a finding that the documents of auction sale are valid until set aside by competent court, but without making any discussion or recording any finding on the above noted legal issue about the legal authority of the Certificate Officer.

22. Direction of the Appellate Division:

As pointed out earlier, in CPLA No. 2113 of 2010, the Appellate Division has sent the Revision on remand with the following observations and directions:

"Moreso, while interfering with a judgment of reversal, it is expected that the High Court Division should have made a cursory glance of the evidence on record for ascertaining as to which findings of fact arrived at by the courts below are correct and also to decide as to whether there is any misreading or non-consideration of the material evidence on record by the court of appeal below, which are legal grounds for interference against the findings of fact in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction."

23. Points to be considered and decided in Revision:

In consideration of the facts of the case, the issues raised in this Revision and the direction of the Appellate Division the following issues are to addressed and decided in this Revision: a. Prime facie title and exclusive possession of the plaintiff vis-a-vis the title and possession claimed by the defendant, b. The legality of the auction sale in a Certificate Case initiated in 1952-53. c. Whether there is any non-consideration or misreading of material evidence by the appellate court.

24. However the nature of controversy between the parties is such that even if the plaintiff is able to prove his prima facie title, it will not yield any result if it is found that the suit land was legally auction sold as claimed by the defendant. So it is convenient to first look into the documents relating to auction sale and the SA Khatian and the legal issues involved in the matter.

25. The disputed auction sale and the SA khatian:

About the auction sale, Defendant No.1 has filed three documents being Exhibit-B,C and D. Exhibit-D is the original Certificate of Sale signed by the Certificate Officer on 18-7-1955 in Certificate Case No. 1227/1952-53. The case was initiated against (1) Arfaner Nessa, (2) Safarun Nessa, (3)

Saydun Nessa, (4) Sayed Ali (5) Tamiz-uddin and several others. It is stated in Exhibit-D that the said three women were daughters of Mon Gazi.

Exhibit-D further shows that the auction purchasers are Ahmed Ullah, Salamatullah, Siddiqur Rahman, Idris and two others and that the sale was confirmed.

Exhibit-C shows that the auction purchasers, on 23-4-1954, filed an application stating that there was an amicable partition of the land auction purchased by them and that the land specified in the various schedules to the application were allocated to specified purchasers.

Exhibit-B shows that, in Misc. Case No. 24 of 1956-57, the said auction purchasers filed requisites (তলবানা-১) for delivery of possession and that an order was passed on 9-8-1956 stating that "possession delivered on 29-6-1956 and the case is disposed of."

26. The certified copy of SA Khatian No. 44 (Exhibit-E) shows that the land of CS khatian No. 23 including suit plot No. 161 was recorded in the names of the auction purchasers i.e. Ahmed Ullah and others, including a certificate debtor Sayad Ali. Exhibit-F, F(1) and F (2) show that rent was paid against the said SA khatian for several years beginning from 1977. It is noted that the Certificate of Sale (Exhibit-D) is silent as to whether it was initiated for arrears of rent or for other reasons. However Exhibit-C contains a reference to the case number as কেস নং ১২২৭ নং ১৯৫২-৫৩ ইং খাং ডিং. The expression খান ডিং is not very clear, but it at best indicates that the abbreviation stands for খাজনা ডিক্রি The defendant No. l, as DW 1, in the line of his written statement, stated that the Certificate Case was initiated due to arrears of rent.

27. In the absence of any better evidence to the contrary, it appears that the certificate case was purportedly initiated for arrears of rent.

28. But on the issue of the legal authority of the Certificate Officer, I agree with Mr Abul Kalam Patwary, the learned advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner, that despite the enactment of the Act, 1950, this Act did not commence before April, 1956 and therefore the rent receiving interest had not vested in the Government authorizing the Government functionaries to realize any arrear of rent that might have fallen due to the landlord. Such rent was not a public demand under the Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913 nor was it otherwise realizable through the Certificate Officer. Thus he had no legal authority to initiate the said case in 1952-53.

<u>29. This legal position is confirmed by section 68C that was inserted in the Act, 1950 by EP Ordinance No. XLIV of 1958. This new section conferred a right on the landlord to realize arrear rent by filing a Rent Suit in the Civil Court.</u>

<u>30. Rent receiving interest of the landlords was acquired by the Government by virtue of section 3 of the Act, 1950. But according to section 3(1) of the Act, 1950 a Gazette Notification was necessary for coming info force of the said section 3 itself. In the district of Comilla and certain "other districts, the Act, 1950 including section-3 came into force on 2nd April, 1956 by Notification dated 2nd April, 1956 published in the Extra Ordinary Gazette (vide Obaidul Huq's the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, Third Edition 2001, page-21, published by DLR.</u>

31. It follows that the auction sale claimed by the defendant No. 1 has no legal basis. Even if the certificate case was initiated and the Certificate of Sale (Exhibit-D) was issued, the entire proceeding was illegal and this document is void ability. The auction purchasers acquired no right or title by virtue of it. The appellate court committed a clear error of law in holding that the auction sale was lawful and that those are valid documents until set-aside in a proper suit.

32. In support of his claim that the auction documents (Exhibits B, C and D) are forged, plaintiff filed in the trial court an information slip dated 24-2-1987, but it was not admitted in evidence. It contains an information that the records of the Certificate Case No. 1227/1952-53 and of Miscellaneous Case No. 24 of 1956-57 were not available in the Record Room of the Collector.

33. In consideration of the claim and counter claim of the parties, an order was passed by this Court on 2-5-2013 that additional evidence would be recorded on the matter and accordingly the Deputy Commissioner, Comilla was directed to produce the case record of the said two cases and the concerned registers, and if any or all of those were not available a report should be sent about such non avail ability

34. In response, the Deputy Commissioner has sent a report under স্মারক নং-০৫.২০.১৯০০.০১৭.০৪.০৩৩.১২, তারিখঃ ২১ জুলাই, ২০১৩ to this court to the effect that the case records or the registers were not available in the record room or in the office of the General Certificate officer, Comilla.

35. In view of such report no witness was summoned for recording additional evidence. Neither of the parties agitated the matter of additional evidence.

36. It appears that the evidence on record is not sufficient to arrive at a decision about the alleged forgery or otherwise. However, as pointed out by Mr Abdul Quddus Mia, the learned Advocate for the defendant. opposite party, irrespective of the legality or otherwise of the Certificate Case, the auction sale has somehow found place in the S.A khatian (Exhibit-E) pre pared in the names of the auction purchasers and even in the name of one of the purported certificate debtor Sayad Ali. It is not clear from the materials on record as to how the name of the said Sayad Ali was included in the S.A khatian.

<u>37. Be that as it may, according to section 144A of the Act, 1950, the entries in the SA khatian are to be presumed as correct and it is also a supporting evidence of possession of the tenants, unless rebutted by better evidence. This aspect of the scenario may be examined vis-a-vis the claim of the parties and the evidence led by them on possession.</u>

38. Possession: In support of his claim, plaintiff produced oral and documentary evidence through four witnesses including himself as PW 1. His documents have been marked a Exhibits 1(series) and Exhibits 2-4.

39. These documents show that deceased plaintiff Rajaban Nessa purchased the suit land by kabala dated 20-02-1954 (Exhibit-1(2)) from Hafizuddin and that the vendor Hafizuddin purchased the same from Yakub son of Nowab Ali by kabala dated 17-4-1950 (Exhibit-1). Plaintiff also filed a rent receipt (Exhibit-2) showing payment of rent by Rostom Ali on 31-03-1959 on behalf of Mon Gazi.

40. It is noted that PW 3 and 4 stated that Rostom was son of Golam Ali, who according to the plaintiff (PW 1), was one of the two domestic servants of Mon Gazi.

41. But Plaintiff could not produce any direct evidence about the oral gift by Mon Gazi to the two domestic servants Nowab Ali and Golam Ali. He produced some indirect evidence, namely the oral testimony through PW2- 4 and the registered Nadabi Patra dated 27-08-1987 (Exhibit-3) executed by the two grand-daughters of Mon Gazi.

42. PW 3, Tamijuddin, aged 70/65 years and PW 4 Bosat Ali Sardar, aged 60 years, both being residents of the suit village, stated that they had seen Nowab Ali and Golam Ali possessing the suit land. They also stated the details about the next generation of the said Nowab and Golam Ali and about the subsequent transfers namely the purchase and possession of Hafizuddin from Yakub son of Nowab and subsequently of Rajaban Nessa from Hafizuddin and finally of the oral gift by Rajaban Nessa to plaintiff No. 1. They further stated that plaintiff No. 1 has been in possession. PW 4 further stated that he was present when Rajaban Nessa (plaintiff No. 2) orally gifted the suit land to plaintiff No. 1 before 2/4 days of her death.

43. In the registered Nadai Pattra dated 27-08-1982 (Exhibit-3) the executants Amena and Abeda have stated that their grand-father Mon Gazi had gifted the suit plot to his two domestic servants Golam Ali and Nowab Ali and that they (Amena and Abeda) did not claim the suit land.

44. Both PW 3 and 4 stated that Mon Gazi had no daughter and that after his death his only son Hari Dhon and finally the grand daughters of Mon Gazi being Amena, Abeda and Sayadun Nessa became the owner of the property left by Mon Gazi. Both the witnesses denied the occurrence of any auction sale.

45. Another witness PW 2, named Abdul Khaleque (defendant No. 2) son of Abdur Rahman, stated that plaintiff No. 1 Wahid is in possession of the suit land and that he ( PW 2) purchased some land from one of the auction purchasers named Idris Mia, but Idris himself did not get delivery of possession of the auction purchased land and consequently PW 2 himself could not get possession from Idris because of the resistance from the plaintiff. He further stated that none of the auction purchasers got delivery of possession of their auction purchase land.

46. The trial Court, upon discussion of the oral and documentary evidence on record, believed the aforesaid three witnesses (PW 2, 3 and 4) with regard to possession of the plaintiff and also believed the fact of oral gift of the entire suit plot by Mon Gazi to his domestic servants Nowab Ali and Golam Ali and the subsequent transfers that led to acquisition of the suit land by plaintiff Wahid. The appellate Court however discarded the testimony of PW 2, Abdul Khaleque, son of Abdur Rahamn on the fallacious reasoning that PW 2 himself purchased some land from one of the auction purchasers Idris. Such reasoning of the appellate-Court is the result of non-consideration of the material part of the statement of PW 2. The appellate court misread the impact of the testimony of PW 2, because in disclosing the truth PW 2 deposed against own interest. For proper appreciation the relevant part of statement of PW 2 is quoted below:

“আমি ২নং বিবাদী৷ নালিশী দাগ বাদী দখল করে ৷ আমি ইদ্রিশ মিয়া হইতে খরিদ করেছিলাম । সে বলেছে নিলাম খরিদ সূত্রে মালিক ৷ নিলাম মূলে কোন সম্পত্তি দখল পাই নাই ৷ নালিশী সম্পত্তি কেউ নিলাম খরিদ মূলে দখল করে নাই ৷

আমি খরিদ করলে বাদী আমাকে দখল দেয় নাই। উক্ত সম্পত্তি অহিদ (plaintiff) দখল করে ৷ আমি ইদ্রিশ মিয়াকে বলেছি টাকা নয়ত জমি দেও ৷ ইদ্রিশ বলে মামলা শেষ হলে একটা হবে ৷ আমি খরিদ করার পূর্বেও নাঃ জমি অহিদ (plaintiff) দখল করিত। ১নং বিবাদী ২-১/২ গন্ডা কিনেছে তাহাতে খালেক (defendant No. 1) দখলে নাই অহিদ দখলে আছে।”

47. The appellate Court discarded the testimony of PW 3 Tamijuddin on the reasoning that he (PW 3) stated that his son named Khaja Mainuddin had auction purchased some land and thus became owner thereof. This reasoning of the appellate Court is the result of non- consideration of the material part of the statement of PW 3 as follows:

Examination-in-chief

“নাঃ জমি আমার বাড়ীর পাশে৷ রজবন নেসার অংশসহ নাল জমি অহিদ দখল করে ৷

নাঃ জমি বিবাদীরা দখল করে না ৷ নাল খতিয়ানে বহু সম্পত্তি আছে ৷ আমি খরিদ করেছি এবং দখলেও আছি ৷ নাঃ জমি নিলাম হয়নি রজবন নেসার কোন ছেলে মেয়ে ছিল না ৷ অহিদকে তিনি মৌখিক দান করে গেছেন ৷ মন গাজীর আরদান, খায়রন্ নেসা, সৈয়দ নেসা নামে কোন মেয়ে ছিল না ৷ মন গাজী হরিধনকে একমাত্র পুত্র ব্লেখে মারা যায় ৷ হরিধানের যেয়ে আবেদা, আমেনা, ও পরিমল নেছা এই তিন মেয়ে........

Cross-examination.

“মামলার জোতে আমার জমি আছে।আমি খরিদ সূত্রে মালিক ৷ হরিধনের মেয়ে আসেন। থেকে সম্পত্তি খরিদ করেছি ৷ দলিল আছে৷

..........খাজা মইনুদ্দীন আমার ছেলে যে নালিশী জোতে মালিক আছে ৷ সে কিভাবে মালিক হয়েছে তাহা জানিনা। আমার ছেলে নিলাম খরিদ করে জমির মালিক আছে।

...১৫৭ দাগের সম্পত্তি মন গাজীর ৷ উহা আমি দখল করি। আমি ও আমার ছেলে একত্রে থাকি। ১৫৭, ১৫৮, ২৮১ দাগ আমার খরিদ সম্পত্তি।

48. It is noted that, in cross-examination, the question of auction purchase of his son was put to PW 3, in view of the contents of Exhibit-C, being the certified copy of the application filed by the auction purchasers stating that there was an amicable partition among themselves and that Khaja Mian Uddin, son of PW 3 was allotted plot Nos. 157, 158 and 281.

49. The appellate court totally misread the evidence of PW 3. Because PW 3 admitted the truth about his son's role only as an auction purchase, but PW 3 eventually denied the title and possession of his son, and asserted his own title and possession over those plots.

50. The appellate Court discarded the testimony of PW 4 Bosot Ali on the reasoning that this witness disowned his signature in the kabala of defendant No. 1(Exhibit-ka) as an attesting witness, but the appellate Court found the signatures of PW 4 on that document and the one on his deposition sheet to be similar.

51. It appears that the appellate Court has failed to consider that it is unsafe to come to a conclusion about similarity of two signatures when it is denied by the purported signatory. Moreover even if the signature of an attesting witness is correct, he is not supposed to know the exact content of document. That cannot be a sound logic for discarding the credibility of PW 4, if his testimony is otherwise credible.

52. The appellate Court also failed to consider the material statement of PW 3, with regard to his own continuous possession of part of the land of the suit khatian by virtue of purchase from the heirs of Mon Gazi. This fact was even supported by the defendant DW 2, Bosot Ali who was produced by the defendant. DW 2 stated that his father Sayad Ali and Tamijuddin (PW 3) are full brothers and they purchased some land in the suit khatian from the original owners and that both are in possession of that land. It is noted that no documents were produced by any of the parties in respect of the aforesaid purchases of P.W. 3 or DW 2's father. However these two witnesses may at best be considered to have some interest in denying the auction sale as they claimed to be purchaser and possessors since before the auction sale. But the testimony of PW 3 and 4 is fully credible when considered with that of PW 2 who in disclosing the truth deposed against his own interest.

53. These statements of PW 2, 3, and 4 prove that even if the auction sale had taken place in paper it was never acted upon in terms of delivery of possession.

54. The fact of non-delivery of possession in consequence of the alleged auction sale is further reflected by the fact that defendant No. 1 to prove his possession did not produce his vendor Salamat Ullah or any other auction purchaser. Nor did Defendant No.1 produce any witness to the fact of delivery of possession through court/certificate office.

55. However to prove his possession defendant himself deposed as DW 1 and also produced DW 2 and 3. All these three witnesses supported the possession of the defendant. They also stated that they heard about delivery of possession after auction sale. The testimony of DW 1 and 3 is not credible. Because both stated that defendant Nb. 2 Abdul Khaleque (PW 2) is in possession of the part of the suit plot by virtue of purchase from auction purchaser Idrish. But this fact was denied by PW 2 Abdul Khaleque himself as quoted earlier.

56. The statement of DW 2 appears to be dubious. Because on one hand he supported defendant's possession on the basis of purchase from an auction purchaser and he again he stated about continuous possession of his father Sayad Ali and Uncle Tamizuddin by virtue of purchase from the heirs of Mon Gazi since before auction.

57. However part of the testimony of DW 2 about his father’s purchase and possession, when considered with the unimpeachable testimony of PW 2, appear to be credible to the extent that delivery of possession as a result of the alleged auction never took place. From the above discussion of the evidence on record I hold that plaintiff has been able to prove his exclusive possession over the suit land by credible testimony of PWs. 1-4 and the indirect admission of DW 2. Defendant No. 1 has failed to prove his possession.

58. The SA khatian was prepared in the names of the auction purchaser including one of the certificate debtor Sayed Ali. But the correctness of the SA khatian as attributed by section 144A of the Act, 1950 is rebutted by better evidence. Because firstly the SA khatian was so prepared on the basis of an illegal certificate case initiated in 1952-53. Secondly the statement of the PW's and DW's prove that the SA khatian does not reflect the reality on the ground about the alleged delivery of possession in 1956 as per Exhibit-C. Consequently the rent receipts of 1977 and after wards (Exhibit-F series) do not add any value to the claim of the defendant about possession.

59. The appellate court failed to consider above legal aspect and the material evidence of PWs 2, 3, 4 and DW 2 with regard to the possession aspect.

Prima facie title of plaintiff:

60. With regard to prima facie title of the plaintiff, I hold that the following facts constitute his prima facie title: a. The credible testimony of PW 3 and 4 to the effect that they had seen the domestic servants Golam Ali and Nowab Ali possessing the suit plot and also seen Hafiz Uddin being the purchaser from Yakub son of Nowab Ali possessing the suit land. b. The admission made by Amena and Abeda (defendant Nos. 3 and 4) in their registered Nadabi deed dated 27-8-1989 (Exhibit-3) to the effect that their grand-father Mon Gazi had gifted the suit plot to the domestic servants named Golam Ali and Nowab Ali and that they do not claim the same. This deed by itself is not a title deed but it credibly supports at least the truth of the oral gift to the said domestic servants, c. The subsequent transfers that took place, namely Yakub son of Nowab Ali by registered kabala dated 17-4-1995 (Exhibit-1) transferred his portion to Hafizuddin and subsequently Hafiz-uddin by registered kabala dated 20-2-1954 (Exhibit-1(2)) transferred the suit land to Rajaban Nessa. d. The credible testimony of PW 3 and 4 to the effect that they had personal knowledge about the oral gift made by Rajaban Nessa to the plaintiff No. 1.

61. It is noted that the defendant has not produced any direct descendant of Mon Gazi or other descendants with regard to the existence of the three daughters of Mon Gazi named Arfannessa and two others. However DW 2 made some statements about the existence of the said daughters. But PW 3 Tamijuddin aged 65 years and PW 4 Bosot Ali aged 60 years, both denied such existence.

62. Whatever is the truth about the existence of the daughters of Mon Gazi, plaintiff does not claim his title or possession through those daughters. So their existence need not be decided for the purpose of deciding plaintiffs prime facie title.

63. Decision: In consideration of the above I hold that defendant failed to prove that the interest of the successors in interest of Mon Gazi extinguished because of the alleged auction sale. On the contrary the plaintiff could prove his prima facie title and exclusive possession and therefore he is entitled to the decree of permanent injunction.

64. The appellate court committed an error of law resulting in an erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice in holding that the auction sale was lawful. The said court also failed to consider material evidence with regard to the above noted two vital issues and consequently the judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court is not sustainable.

65. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The judgment and decree dated 28-4-1998 passed by the learned Joint district Judge, 1st  court Comilla in Title Appeal No. 118 of 1987 is hereby set-aside with the result that the Judgment and decree dated 28-7-1-87 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Additional Court Sadar, Comilla in Title Suit No. 59 of 1986 is upheld.

No order as to cost.

Send down the lower court records with a copy of this Judgment.

End.
