case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 11th March, 1985 passed by the High Court Division, Chittagong Bench, in Second Appeal No. 296 of 1975)
full_judgment:
A.T.M. Afzal, J: In this appeal by leave the defendants are the appellants. It arises from judgment and decree dated 11th March, 1985 passed by a Single Judge of the High Court Division (Chittagong Bench) in Second Appeal No. 226 of 1975, setting aside the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court and restoring those of the trial Court passed in other Suit No. 156 of 1970.

2. Plaintiff-respondent No. 1 instituted the aforesaid suit in the second Court of the Assistant Judge, Satkania, for permanent injunction alleging, inter alia, that the suit land measuring 3. 23 acres under R.S. Khatian No. 836 belonged to one Fazar Ali in Korfa right and the raiyati right thereof belonged to Emdad Ali. Fazar Ali got mortgaged the suit land to one Jebunnessa and Basharat Ali by a registered deed dated 23.7.1921 and inducted them into possession of the suit land. Emdad Ali filed a rent suit against the heirs of Fazar Ali and the kot-mortgagees and got decree on 28.7.1938. During the pendency of the rent suit widow of Fazar Ali on her own behalf and on behalf of some minor children of said Fazar Ali executed a yearly kabuliyat relationg to 1.61 acres out of the suit land on 29.6.1938 in favour of Nurddin, predecessor of the defendant-appellants. A case was filed before the Debt Settlement Board for releasing the said kot mortagage which was executed by said Fazar Ali. That case was pending even after the passing of the rent decree in favour of Emdad Ali. The rent decree could not be executed as it was stayed by the Debt Settlement Board. However, when the stay order was vacated, in the rent execution Case No.1225 of 1938 the tenancy was auction sold on 10.9.1956 and the predecessor of the plaintiff, one Abdul Latif purchased the same in auction and took delivery of possession on 5.1.1957 and also annulled the encumbrances under Section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act namely, the interest of said Nuruddin, predecessor of the appellants. The said Abdul Latif mutated his name and paid rent.

3. Thereafter, the auction-purchaser sold the suit land to the plaintiff by a kabala dated 27.11.60 and put him into possession. The defendant, however, theatened to dispossess the plaintiff and hence the suit.

4. The defendant Nuruddin died during the pendency of the suit and his heirs contested the same by filing a written statement. Upon denying the plaintiffs allegation, they asserted that the heirs of Fazar Ali first gave verbal lease to Nuruddin in the year 1936, accepted nazar and rents and placed him into possession of 1.61 acres out of the disputed land. Thereafter, the heirs of Fazar Ali, i.e. wife Bakumjan for hereself and on behalf of some of her minor children granted registered patta dated 29.6.38 and dakhilas in vavour of Nuruddin. He was in possession of 1.60 acres on payment of rent and he got corrected the record of right under Section 50 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Plaintiffs vendor Abdul Latif raised objection there but it was rejected. Plaintiffs vendor earlier instituted a suit, O.S. 235 of 1957, against Nuruddin for declaration of his title to the suit land which was dismissed on 2.7.1959.

5. The defendant's further case is that the wholesale acquisition of rent receiving interest took place on 14.4.1956 and Nuruddin became direct tenant under the Government on and from 14.4.1956 prior to the rent sale on 10.9.56 on due payment of rent to the Government from 1363 B.S.  (1956 to 1981). Therefore, the rent sale was nothing but a money sale. The defendants being direct tenants under the Government was not an encumbrance nor it was an annullable one.

6. It was also contended that the papers filed by the plaintiff are all false and fraudulent documents, that the plaintiff or his vendor Abdul Latif had neither possession nor title to the suit land and as such the suit was liable to be dismissed.

7. The learned Assistant Judge, by judgment and decree dated 25.5.74 decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff has been able to prove his title and possession. On appeal by defendant No. 1 (ka), the learned Subordinate Juge, second Court, Chittagong by judgment and decree dated 30.4.75, reversed the decree of the trial Court and dismissed the suit.

8. Plaintiff then took a second appeal as already mentioned above and succeeded in getting the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court restored.

9. Leave was granted to consider whether the question of title and possession has been decided by the trial Court and the learned Judge of the High Court Division in a proper legal and factal perspective and upon correct principles as are required to be followed in a suit only for permanent injunction.

10. It has been noticed that the plaintiff brought the suit for permanent injunction upon assertion of title to the suit land on the basis of an auction purchase made by his vendor, Abdul Latif in Rent Execution Case No. 1225 of 1938 on 10.9.1956. The auction-purchaser. allegedly took delivery of possession of the suit land on 5.1.1957.

11. It appears that both the trial Court and the learned judge of the High Court Division while dealing with the question of title totally failed to take notice of the relevant provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950, briefly the Act, pertaining to the provisions relating to arrear rents etc. and their realisation which accured prior to their vesting in the Government under Clause (C) of Sub-section (4) of section 3 or under Clause (7) of Section 44 of the Act. The learned Assistant Judge thoroughly misdirected himself in taking the view that the rent suit, execution proceeding etc. were to continue under the old law i.e. the Bengal Tenancy Act notwithstanding the promulgation of the Act in 1951. He observed that the sale in question could be held legally and validly under the old law by reason of Section 6 and 7 of the General Clauses Act. Having further found that there was a valid rent sale on 10.9.56 and Abdul Latif obtained delivery of possession from the judgment debtors, it was held that the plaintiffs title was genuine and true.

12. The learned judge of the High Court Division considered the various documents filed by the plaintiff, particularly Ext. 3, the sale certificate, ext. 4, Order of the Munsif in Rent Execution Case No. 125 of 1938, Ext. 5, writ of delivery of possession, Ext. 6, R.S. Khatian, Ext. 7, P.S. Khatian, Ext. 8 series, dakhilas and Ext. 110, Kabala dated 27.11.1960 and found that these documents clearly indicated the prima facie title of the plaintiff in the suit land. There was no consideration whatever as to the validity or otherwise of the plaintiff was based. It is, therefore, necessary to refer to the relevant provisions of the Act in order to see whether the alleged rent sale could at all take place on 10.9.1956.

13. The Act originally in Chapter 9 made “provisions relating to arrears of revenue, rent and cesses". Section 62(1) thereof reads as follows:

"62(1) All arrears of rent and all cesses and interest, which have vested in the Provincial Government under clause (c) of Sub-section (4) of Section 3 or under clause (7) of Section 44, shall be payable to the Provincial Government and not to anybody else; and no payment made in contravention of this Sub-section shall be valid.

Section 63 then reads:

"63. If any suit or proceeding for the recovery of any arrears which have vested in the Provincial Government under clause (c) of Sub-section (4) of Section 3 or under clause (7) of Section 44 or any proceeding in execution of a decree for the recovery of any such arrears is pending before any Civil Court on the date or day, as the case may be, referred to in the said clauses, such suit or proceeding shall not be further proceeded with and shall be deemed to have been withdrawn, and any such decree may be executed as if it were a certificate filed under the Bengal Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913."

14. It is not disputed that the proceeding of the Rent Execution Cast No. 1225 of 1938 was pending on the date of the Notification under Section 3 of the Act (2nd April, 1956). In terms of aforesaid Section 63, therefore, the proceeding in question could not be further continued and was deemed to have been withdrawn and the decree could be executed only under the Public Demands Recovery Act.

15. Then there came Ordinance No. III of 1956. The East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956, which came into force on 22 March, 1956, adding a new Chapter, IXA, providing for "Special Provisions relating to arrears of rent." For our present purpose the provisions of Section 68B thereof only are relevant which read thus:

"68B. (1) When a decree for arrears of rent and cesses referred to in sub-section (1) of Section 68A has been passed, whether before or after the date on which the interests of a rent-receiver have vested in the Provincial Government under Section 3 or Section 4, in any suit instituted before the said date by such rent receiver for the recovery of such arrears, such decree shall, notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, be executed in the manner provided in this section and not otherwise.

(2) Every such decree holder may apply in the prescribed manner and withing the prescribed period to the Revenue Officer referred to in Sub-section (2) of Section 68A for the execution of such decree and such Revenue Officer shall on receipt of such application, if satisfied that the decree is not barred by limitation execute such decree as if it were a certificate under the Bengal Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913, and the provisions of Sub-section (3) of section 68A shall apply to the execution of such decree.

(3) Where any proceedings in execution of a decree referred to in Sub-section (1) is pending in any Court on the date on which the interests of such decree-holder have become vested in the Provincial Government under Section 3 or Section 44, such execution proceedings shall abate and such decree-holder may apply for the execution of such decree in the manner provided in Sub-section (2)."

16. Mr. Nurullah, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent, has not disputed that the said Ordinance Ill of 1956 held the field when the alleged auction sale took placede and delivery of possession was given pursuant thereto. In view of the clear provision in Section 68B(3) Mr. Nurullah could not but admit that the rent execution proceeding in question stood abated at the relevant time and as such the sale etc. therein were void abinitio. The learned Advocate also fairly submitted that the trial Court being under a misconception of law and the learned judge of the High Court Division having failed to notice the aforesaid provisions of the Act, their findings as to the title of the plaintiff cannot, be legally sustained. Even so, the learned Advocate argued that the plaintiff's possession having been found, there was no illegality in granting the decree for permanent injunction.

<u>17. It is true that in a suit of the present mature the question of title is relevant only incidentally and no primarily. It is the actual possession of the plaintiff which must be proved and the main part or the most main of the evidence must be directed to that end. It is well settled that even a trespasser's possession is good and valid against the entire world except the true owner and such possession is entitled to protection until he is evicted by due process of law. Therefore, one has to consider the evidence of actual possession mainly in a suit of the instant kind.</u>

18. It has been noticed by the Courts below and we have also seen that so far as documentary evidence is concerned relationg to payment of rent, record of right etc. the case of both the parties seem to stand at par. One of the grievances made by the learned Advocate for the appellants, however, is that the defendants documents, namely, Ext. B. C, D, E, G and H series were not at all considered by the learned Judge of the High Court Division. That this grievance has substance cannot be denied inasmuch as no reference is to be found to the said documents in the impugned judgment of the High Court Division. It appears that of the defendants' documents, the learned Judge of the High Court Division only considered Ext. A, certified copy of the patta dated 29.6.38 and observed, inter alia, that the same was completely demolished by the notice of the auction-purchaser under Section 167 of the B.T. Act. In view of the relevant provision of law referred to above, it is hardly necessary to point out that the notice under Section 167 B.T. Act was merely an exercise in futility. The documents and papers relating to auction sale and delivery of possession could hardly be of any help to the plaintiff for proving his possession. In the same manner, the P.S. Khatian, the dakhilas, although evidence of possession could hardly advance his case of actual possession of the suit land for the simple reason that the defendants had as much khatian and dakhilas in their names as were sufficient to match those of the plaintiffs. Among the large number of documents filed by the defendants showing mutation and payment of rent by them, reference may be made to Ext. C(2) which is a copy of the order sheet of Misc. Case No. 344 of 1964 under Section 50 of the Act. It appears that at the instance of Nuruddin, predecessor of the defendants the Revenue Officer ordered that 8 annas of Plot No. 2110 (i.e. 1.61 acres) be transferred to his Khatian No. 1215. Ext.C(3), E, E(1) F consistently support the defendant's case in respect of their share claimed out of the suit land. Dakhilas Ext. B series and H series are there in support of the defendants' case. However, we do not think that such documents proved on either side were such upon which actual possession could be decided. The plaintiff was at a disadvantage with his documents relating to his title for the reasons already stated. It was incumbent upon him to prove actual possession, by adducing oral evidence sufficient enough to carry conviction firstly, by his vendor Abdul Latif and then by himself. It will be seen that in order to prove possession plaintiff only examined himself as P.W.1 and his brother-in-law Badi Ahmed, P.W.2 and nobody else, Defendants on their part also examined two witnesses. In the facts and circumstances of the case noticed above it must be said that the evidence adduced by the plaintiff was not only meagre but wholly unconvincing for the purpose of proving actual possession in the suit land. Indeed there was no independent and reiable evidence on the side of the plaintiff to support his case of possession.

19. Looking to the judgment of the trial Court it will be seen how perfunctorily the question of actual possession of the plaintiff was considered before passing a decree for permannent injunction. The relevant part of the judgment reads thus:

"Moreover plaintiff examined P.W.1 (?) who corroborate the possession of plaintiff. Defence of-course filed some dakhilas of past rent, thus (?) he took lease in the year 1936-38 and also examined witnesses for possession. Under the facts and circumstances of this case I have reasons to doubt their genuinity. Considering all these aspects of this case I have been constrained to opine that plaintiff has been able to prove his title and possession and defence has failed to prove his own."

20. So far as the impugned judgment of the High Court Division is concerned, there is no consideration of any oral evidence except saying that the trial Court has believed the evidence of possession by the P.Ws. The learned Judge of the High Court Division failed to consider that in the facts and circumstances of the case the oral evidence of possession as adduced by the plaintiff was utterly inadequate, skimpy and just not legally sufficient for granting a decree of permanent injunction. We have no manner of doubt that had the learned Judge of the High Court Division been aware of the legal provisions referred to above which under the documents (relating to rent sale etc.) relied upon and proved by the plaintiff to be of little value as far as possession is concerned and further if it was noticed that except that of the plaintiff and his brother-in-law there was no independent evidence of possession, the suit could not have been decreed. We are clearly of the opinion that in the facts and circumstances of the case, the evidence adduced is plainly insufficient to sustain a decree for permanent injunction. For the reasons stated above the impugned judgment and decree cannot be allowed to stand.

21. In the result, therefore, this appeal is allowed with costs. The impugned judgment and decree are set aside and the suit is dismissed.

End.

case_source: From the Judgment and Order dated 24.8.89 passed by the High Court Division, Rangpur Bench, in Civil Revision No.63 of 1986.
full_judgment:
M.H. Rahman, J : Respondents filed a suit, S.C.C. Suit No. 1 of 1982 in the Court of Munsif, Second Court, Serajganj, for the eviction of the defendants-appellants from the suit premises. That suit was decreed ex-parte on 9th March, 1983. On 11th August, 1983, the appellants filed Miscellaneous Case No. 77 of 1983 under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with Section 17 of the Small Cause Courts Act, 1887, for setting aside the ex-parte decree. On that date the appellants application praying for exemption from depositing the security money till the hearing of the miscellaneous case was also allowed. The case was fixed for peremptory hearing on 30th July, 1984, but the appellants took time on that date and on several subsequent dates. On 31st December, 1985, the appellants filed a security bond with an application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act read with Section 151 of the Code for acceptance of the bond on condonation of delay. The S.S.C. Judge refused to condone the delay, rejected the security bond and dismissed the Miscellaneous case as not maintainable. In revision the High Court Division upheld the order of the learned S.C.C. Judge.

2. The appellants now want to rely on their application dated 11th August, 1983, and the order that was passed on that application. The Court allowed the prayer of the appellants for exemption but did not give any direction nor fix any time for the deposit of the security money. It is contended that the trial Court and the revisional Court failed to notice the appellants' application dated 11th August, 1983, and the S.S.C. Judge's order passed thereon on the same date. It is submitted that the learned S.C.C. Judge did not indicate any time within which the security deposit was to be made; that there was an open-ended extension of time by the Court itself and there was no delay or laches on the part of the appellants and that there was sufficient compliance with the requirements of the proviso to Section 17(1) of the Small Cause Courts Act, when they filed the security bond on 31st December, 1985, for acceptance on condonation of delay. It is contended that if there were a mistake in passing the relevant order on 11th August, 1983, the mistake was that of the Court.

3. It appears that the petitioner's application dated 11th August, 1983 and the order passed by the Court were not brought to the notice of the High Court Division. The appellants did not themselves rely on that order before the trial Court and that is why they filed an application for acceptance of the security bond on condonation of delay.

4. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division observed that at the time of the presentation of the application under Section 17 of the S.C.C. Act, the appellants did not furnish the security deposit nor did make any application seeking the necessary direction of the Court; that after a lapse of about 2 years and 8 months they made a prayer for time to furnish the requisite security; that the S.C.C. Judge refused the prayer and set down the case for hearing on 26th December, 1985, but even on that day the appellants made no attempt to furnish the security and that when the matter came up again for hearing on 31st December, 1985, they filed a security bond with a prayer for its acceptance after condonation of delay.

5. It is true that on 11th August, 1983, the petitioner's prayer for exemption was allowed till the hearing of the Miscellaneous case. The Miscellaneous case came up for the premptory hearing on 30th July, 1984, and thereafter several dates were fixed for peremptory hearing, but the appellants did not comply with the requirements under proviso to Section 17(1) on or before the date when the matter was fixed for pre-emptory hearing.

<u>6. The Court can extend time for compliance with the proviso to Section 17(1), but it cannot give an extension of time till the hearing of the matter, as wrongly granted in this case, as that would frustrate the very purpose of that proviso. This is not a case where the litigant suffers from the wrong order of the Court. This is case where a defaulter wants to take advantage of an order wrongly passed by the Court. We find it difficult to understand why there was so much delay in filing a security bond, rather a simple matter. The delay was due to negligence and the learned S.C.C. Judge rightly refused to condone the same.</u>

7. We do not like to interfere on the ground of the technicalities, now urged but not raised or urged before the High Court Division. Besides, the consideration of such technicalities will ensure to the benefit of a defaulter who resorted to a stratagem for an exemption not allowable under the law.

8. The appeal dismissed with cost.

End.

full_judgment:
Syed Fazle Ahmed, J.: This Rule call in question the order dated 6.11.85 passed by Upazila Munsif, Durgapur in Misc. Case No. 54 of 1984 arising out of O.C. Suit No. 175 of 1983 allowing the petition under Order 1 Rule 10 of the C.P.C.

2. Facts giving rise to this Rule be stated briefly thus:

Petitioner as plaintiff instituted a suit for cancellation of the deed of Hiba-bil-Ewaj dated 17.3.1980 and prior to consideration of that suit, petitioner as plaintiff filed a partition suit being Partition Suit No. 81 of 1971 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Rajshahi: That Opposite Party No. 1 and his brother late Bades Molla did not appear in the Partition Suit and accordingly plaintiff petitioner obtained a preliminary decree in respect of certain share and obtained final decree on 25.7.75 and got delivery of possession through court as per separate saham on 26.7.80 and got his name mutated in the Govt. acquired Estate.

3. Thereafter, defendant opposite party made a proposal to this petitioner for exchange of some land from the saham of the petitioner and on good faith the petitioner agreed to the proposal of exchange of land. When the plaintiff petitioner went to take possession of his exchanged, land defendant opposite party did not hand over the possession of the exchanged land and on verification of the deed, it came to light that petitioner's own land is shown in the schedule of the ewaj deed but the land given in T.S. No. 175 of 1983, does not belong to defendant, opposite party and by that deed of ewaj, opposite party committed fraud and petitioner has been highly prejudiced and so the plaintiff petitioner filed a suit for cancellation of the deed of Hiba-bil-Ewaj and that suit was decreed ex-parte on 6.6.83 in favour of the plaintiff petitioner.

4. On 15.3.84 an application under Order 9 Rule 13 C.P.C was filed for setting aside the ex-parte decree passed in Misc. Case No. 54 of 1984, which was initiated by opposite party to have the ex-parte decree set aside and the plaintiff petitioner contested the aforesaid Misc. Case by filing written objection. During pendence of the Misc. Case No. 54 of 1984 opposite party No.1 Badesh Molla full brother of opposite party No. 1 and of petitioner No. 2 of the Misc. case had died on 6.9.94 and substitution was not made in time and the plaintiff petitioner filed a petition on 5.9.85 praying for passing an order of abatement on account of delay occurred in the matter of substitution of the legal heirs of late Badesh Molla and since the substitution was not made within statutory period of 90 days the case as a whole abated.

5. Subsequently, opposite party made a prayer on 6.11.85 for addition of parties under Order 1 Rule 10 C.P.C. The petition filed by the plaintiff petitioner praying passing order of abatement of the Misc. Case and the application for addition of parties were taken up by the learned Munsif together. The prayer for addition of parties made under Order 1 Rule 10 C.P.C. was allowed but the learned Munsif rejected prayer for passing an order of abatement. It is under the circumstances plaintiff petitioner having felt aggrieved by the impugned order, moved the revisions jurisdiction of this court and obtained the present Rule.

6. The learned Advocate Mr. M.A. Sobhan appears for the petitioner, but none appears on behalf of the opposite party.

7. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has attacked the order allowing the application under Order 1 Rule 10 C.P.C. as illegal and contrary to law inasmuch as without setting aside the order of abatement the prayer for addition of parties is not entertainable in law. It is further submitted that since substitution was not made within statutory period the proceeding as a whole already abated and the learned Munsif committed gross illegality in allowing the prayer, for addition or parties without getting abatement set aside. It is further submitted that the ex-parte decree dated 6.6.83 passed in O.C. Suit No. 175 of 1983 is indivisible inasmuch as by that decree the deed of ewaj was held to the fraudulent and so the decree to be treated as indivisible and the observation made by the learned Munsif that Misc. Case abated partially is wholly unwarranted and contrary to law.

<u>8. Since the contention urged by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff petitioner appears to be well founded and since that contention remains unchallenged and unopposed because of non-appearance of the learned Advocate for opposite party, contention urged by the learned Advocate for the petitioner will stand firmly. Petitioner No. 1 was aware of the death of petitioner No. 2 Badesh Molla and that no step was taken within the statutory period to have the heirs of deceased Badesh Molla substituted and since the decree passed in O.C. Suit No. 175 of 1983 is indivisible, the Misc. Case will stand abated as a whole and unless this abatement is set aside the order for addition of parties cannot legally be passed.</u>

9. It may be mentioned here that an application was made before the Upazila Munsif on 5.9.85 informing him that Badesh Mollah died on 6.9.84 and his heirs having not been substituted within the statutory period of 90 days, the case as a whole stands abated. But the learned Munsif did not take cognizance of this application filed plaintiff petitioner and no order was passed.

10. In the result, the impugned order passed by the Upazila Munsif, Durgapur, in Misc. Case No. 54 of 1984 allowing the petition under Order 1 Rule 10 C.P.C. is hereby set aside and the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the judgment and decree dated 27-4-2003 passed by the learned Additional District Judge in charge, Court No. 8, Dhaka, in Title Appeal No. 123 of 2002 allowing the appeal, decreeing the suit on reversing those dated 31-1-2002 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, in Title Suit No. 239 of 2001 dismissing the suit.

2. Facts necessary for disposal of the Rule are that the Opposite Party Nos. 1 and 2 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 239 of 2001 in the Court of Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka praying for a decree for Specific Performance of Contract contending, inter alia, that the suit house being House No. 10, Road No.2, Block No. H, Section No. 2, of mouza Senpara Parbata, under Sub-Registry Office Mirpur, District-Dhaka belonged to Mirpur Housing Estate. Said Housing Estate offered to sell the same in favour of the defendant No.1 at a consideration of Taka 96,843. The defendant was directed to pay his first installment amounting to Tk. 19,369 but he being unable to pay that installment made an offer to the plaintiff No. 2's father, Harunur Rashid, the full brother of the plaintiff, for purchase of the said housing plot. Accordingly, Harunur Rashid agreed upon to purchase the said house and paid the first installment amounting to Taka 19,369. Similarly, paid all other instalments dated 12-1-1986, 7-3-1987, 6-10-1987, 19-6-1998 and made the payment of Taka 96,843 in full. Thereafter, the concerned Authority executed and registered a transfer deed in favour of the defendant No. 1 dated 15-9-1988. It is the further case of the plaintiff that the plaintiff's father Harunur Rashid paid the costs incurred towards registration amounting to Tk. 1877 and also spent the costs towards mutation in the name of the defendant No.1 amounting to Tk. 3000. There was an oral stipulation that the defendant No. 1 would live in the suit house till a sale deed is executed and registered in favour of the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 who are the sister's son and son of Harunur Rashid (PW 1). It is the further case that on 23-8-1996 the defendant No. 1 executed an agreement in favour of the plaintiff for transfer of the suit land pursuant to the oral agreement dated 15-11-1984. On that date the other documents in respect of suit house was handed over in favour of Harunur Rashid and the possession of the house was also handed over. The plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 have constructed a tin-shed house upon the said land and have been in possession through Bharatia. They paid the city corporation holding taxes, gas bills and water bills and they have been in possession in the suit house since 23-8-1996. It is their further case that as per oral contract dated 15-11-1984, the defendant No. 1 applied to the Housing Authority on 10-9-1996 for permission to transfer the suit house in favour of the plaintiffs and the defendant No. 1 was directed to attend before the defendant No. 5 with all necessary papers fixing 31-10-1996, but the defendant No. 1 could not attend due to bad eye sight. The plaintiff No. 2's father spent necessary costs towards operation of his eyes and he regained his eye sight. It is the further case of the plaintiffs that the defendant No.2 being accompanied by some terrorists and being armed with deadly weapons threatened the plaintiff's father on 16-2-2000 at 3-30 PM and blasted a bomb which compelled the plaintiff's father (PW 1) to lodge a GD Entry being No. 1239 dated 16-2-2000 and 16-10-2000 with the Mirpur Police Station. The defendant's making some conspiracy for dispossessing the plaintiffs from the suit house whereupon another GD. Entry being No. 1497 dated 19-10-2000 was lodged with the Mirpur Police Station. The defendant Nos. 2-3 disclosed that the defendant No. 1 has transferred the suit house in their favour by a Heba deed dated 18-10-2000. Thereafter, the plaintiff No. 2's father Harunur Rashid (PW 1) requested the defendant Nos. 1-3 on 6-11-2000 to execute and register a kabala deed in favour of the plaintiffs pursuant to the oral contract dated 15-11-1984 and that was refused and, as such, the suit.

3. The defendant Nos, 1-3 contested the suit by filing a Written Statement denying the plaint's case and totally denying the existence of any oral contract and contending, inter alia, that the story of oral contract is false. There was no contract as alleged in the plaint. The suit is barred by limitation. The plaintiffs have not come up with clean hands. The further case of the defendants are that the defendant No.1 got the suit property from the Government. The Government decided to sell the said suit property to the defendant No.1 at a cost of Tk. 96,843. The defendant No.1 is an employee under the PWD and paid the entire amount from his own pocket in different installments and, as such, the Government executed the sale deed in his favour vide deed No. 6369 dated 15-9-1988. Once, he was suddenly attacked with strong eye disease in both the eyes and was about to become blind. At that stage his sons, the defendant Nos. 2-3, were not grown up enough to understand the official processes. At that time he had to take help of his younger brother i.e. the father of the plaintiff No.2, to assist him to get completed the execution and registration of the sale deed in his favour from the Government. Thereafter, he intended to transfer the suit property in favour of his sons, the defendant Nos. 2-3, and taking the advantage of the defective eyesight of the defendant No.1, the father of the plaintiff No.2 Harunur Rashid (PW 1) started conspiracy to grab the suit property and with that view, he committed theft in the house of the defendants and took away their original documents from his house, beyond his knowledge. The defendant No.1 lodged a GD Entry on 18-6-2000 with Mirpur Police Station. The defendant No.1 got back his eyesight after taking surgical operation and could detect that although he filed application for transfer-permission in favour of his sons, the defendant Nos. 2-3, but that application was replaced by another application for transfer in favour of the plaintiffs. Thereafter, he filed another application on 28-6-2000 for getting permission to transfer of the suit house in favour of his sons, the defendant Nos. 2-3. Thereafter, the Commissioner of Settlement after verification of all those facts found that the defendants Nos. 1-3 are in possession in the suit house with valid title. So, they granted permission dated 10-10-2000 vide Memo No. 728/61/8547/1(4) for transfer of the suit properties in favour of the defendant Nos. 2-3. On the basis of the said permission, the defendant No. I has transferred the suit properties in favour of his sons, the defendant Nos. 2-3, on 18-10-2000 vide Heba deed No. 6206 within the knowledge of the plaintiffs and also within the knowledge of said Harunur Rashid. As a result, the ill intention of Md Harunur Rashid (PW 1) came to an end. The defendants No. 1-3 are enjoying the suit properties by making constructions as per their own arrangements. They are using a portion of the premises as their dwelling house and another portion has been let out to the tenants. Thereafter, said Harunur Rashid, ie. the father of the plaintiff No.2, by using the name of the plaintiffs, had filed the aforementioned suit for Specific Performance of Contract. He also filed a false case against the defendant Nos. 1-3 on 23-12-2000 with the Mirpur Police Station being Mirpur PS Case No. 83(12)2000 under sections 143/448/ 323/379/506 of the Penal Code and on the plea of the aforesaid case, the PW 1 with the help of local police, started conspiracy against the defendants so that they are compelled to hide themselves until bail is granted. Thereafter, Harunur Rashid trespassed into the suit premises on 23-12-2000 during the pendency of the said criminal case. Thereafter, the matter was brought to the notice of the learned Assistant Judge. The defendant Nos. 1-3 also filed a petition for restoration of possession before the learned Assistant Judge on 24-6-2001 and that application was kept with the record for disposal. The defendants No.1-3 also filed a suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession against the said Harunur Rashid (PW 1) and his men before the learned Assistant Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka being Title Suit No. 118 of 2002 which on transfer is still pending before the learned Assistant Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka as being Title Suit No. 116 of 2003.

4. Upon the pleadings of the parties the learned .Assistant Judge framed the following issues:

(i) Is the suit maintainable as it stands framed?

(ii) Is the suit barred by limitation?

(iii) Whether the relief sought for by the plaintiffs is just?

(iv) Whether the plaintiff is entitled to get a decree for Specific Performance of Contract on the basis of oral contract?

5. The plaintiffs examined 10 PWs and their documentary evidences were marked as Exhibit 1-27(ka). On the other hand, the defendants examined 5 DWs and their documentary evidences were marked as Exhibit ka-Dha.

6. The learned Assistant Judge on consideration of the evidence on record dismissed the suit by the judgment and decree dated 31-1-2002 holding that the plaintiffs could not prove the case of oral contract.

7. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and decree the plaintiffs preferred Title Appeal No. 123 of 2002 and the said appeal was heard by the learned Additional District Judge in charge, Court No. 8, Dhaka, who by the impugned judgment and decree dated 27-4-2003 allowed the appeal, decreed the suit on reversing the judgment of the trial Court.

8. Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and decree the defendants-petitioners have obtained the instant Rule.

9. Mr Md Ahia, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, took me to the judgments of the Courts below and submitted that the learned Additional District Judge being the last Court of fact has failed to discuss and consider the evidences of the defendant. He further submitted that the appellate Court has given more emphasis upon the Exhibit 4 and accepting that Exhibit 4. to be a proof of oral contract has decreed the suit. He further submitted that the learned Additional District Judge illegally has given more emphasis upon the evidence of PW 7, the mother of the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 and decreed the suit. He submitted that in fact, the evidence of PW 7 does not support any oral agreement. He further submitted that admittedly the plaintiff No.2 being a minor was not entitled to file any suit for Specific Performance of Contract and the Court of appeal has miserably failed to consider this aspect. In support of his contention he relied upon the case law of Julhash Mollah versus Ramani Kanta Malo, reported in 47 DLR (AD) 35. Mr Ahia further submitted that the suit is barred by limitation in view of the fact that the alleged oral contract was dated 15-11-1984 and the suit was filed on 14-11-2000. He lastly submitted that the evidence of the PWs if be read together those do not support the plaintiffs' case of oral contract.

10. Mr TH Khan, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties, on appearing before this Court, submitted that the Court of appeal, being the last Court of fact have considered the evidence on record very judicially and believed that the defendant No.1 executed the Exhibit-4 and agreed upon to transfer the suit house in favour of the plaintiffs. He further submitted that possession of the suit house was handed over in favour of the plaintiffs on 23-8-1996. He further submitted that the learned Additional District Judge most judicially found the existence of oral contract and there is nothing to interfere. He further submitted that the minor is entitled to enforce a contract if that contract is found for the benefit of the minor. He also relied upon the case law reported in 47 DLR (AD) 35. He further submitted that the suit was not barred by limitation in view of the fact that admittedly the plaintiffs have been in possession in the suit house on and from 23-8-1996 and the suit was filed within 3(three) years from the date of refusal of performance of the contract. He prayed for discharge of the Rule.

11. I have heard the learned Advocates of both the parties and have considered their respective submissions. I have perused the judgments of the Courts below and the evidence on record, both oral and documentary very carefully.

12. From the plaint it appears that the plaintiff has filed the suit for specific performance of an oral contract by substantiating following relief:

“(ক) ২নং বাদীর পিতার সহিত ১নং বিবাদীর মৌকিক চুক্তির ভিত্তিতে এবং পরবর্তীতে ১নং বিবাদী কর্তৃক বাদীদের বরাবরে সম্পাদিত গত ২৩-৮-১৯৯৬ইং তারিখের অঙ্গীকার নামার শর্ত অনুযায়ী বাদীদের বরাবরে নালিশী বাড়ীর সাফ কবলা দলিল সম্পাদন ও রেজিষ্ট্রি করিয়া দেওয়ার নিমিত্তে ১-৩ নং বিবাদীদের বিরুদ্ধে চক্তি প্রবলের ডিক্রি দিতে;

(খ)১-৩ নং বিবাদী আদালত কর্তৃক নির্ধারিত সময়ের মধ্য বাদীদের বরাবরে নালিশী বাড়ীর সাফ কবলা দলিল সম্পাদন ও বেজিষ্ট্রি করিয়া দিতে ব্যার্থ হইলে আদালোতযোগে নালিশি বাড়ীর সাফ কবলা দলিল বাদীদের বরাবরে সম্পাদন ও রেজিষ্ট্রি করিয়া দিতে;

(গ) মোকদ্দমার খরচ ১-৩ নং বিবাদী বহন করিবে মর্মে ১-৩ নং বিবাদীদের বিরুদ্ধে ডিক্রি দিতে;

(ঘ) আইন ও ন্যায় নীতিতে বাদীগন আরও যে যে প্রতিকার পাইতে পারে তাহার ডিক্রি দিতে মর্জি হয়।

13. On perusal of the plaint, it appears that the plaintiffs have filed the suit only on the basis of an alleged oral contract dated 15-11-1984 and thereafter, on the strength of the written agreement dated 23-4-96 (Exhibit 4). To prove the said oral contract, the Exhibit 4 was admitted into evidence as being subsequent development of the said contract alleging, inter alia, that pursuant to the oral contract, the defendant No.1 entered into a written agreement agreeing upon to execute and register a sale deed in favour of the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2. In a suit for Specific Performance of Contract the plaintiff has to prove the fact of his oral contract very strictly including time, place and manner of entering into the oral contract with very reliable evidences and the Court must scrutinise the oral agreement cautiously. Although the oral agreement was not barred by any law but such oral agreement has to be taken with a grain of salt and has to be looked at with some suspicion unless proved by very reliable evidence and has to be scrutinised very closely.

14. On perusal of the appellate Court's judgments it appears that the learned Additional District Judge in charge, 8th Court, Dhaka did not discuss any oral evidence. He simply accepted the Exhibit 4 to be the main documents in support of the plaintiffs' case and relied upon the evidence of PW 7, the mother of the PW 1 and DW 1. Let us consider as to whether the learned Additional District Judge was justified in decreeing the suit on relying upon the evidence of PW 7 and considering the Exhibit 4.

15. It is evident from the record that the plaintiffs of the suit did not come forward to depose before the Court at the trial and the prove to oral contract. There are 2(two) plaintiffs in the suit. The plaintiff No. 2 is the full sister's son of the PW 1 and the plaintiff No. 2 is the minor son of PW 1. It is further evident from the evidence of PW 1 that he wanted to establish a case that he himself entered into the oral contract dated 15-11-84 to purchase the suit land.

16. From the evidence adduced by the PW 1 it appears that with a view to prove this case of oral contract he has added, in his examination-in-chief the following evidences

“নাঃ জমিটি পরিত্যক্ত জমি ছিল। নাঃ বাড়ীটি সরকারের নিকট হতে বিক্রির প্রস্তাব পায় ১নং বিবাদী ৷ এই সেই বিক্রির প্রস্তাব স্মারক নং ১২৬০ তাং ২৮-১০-৮৪। আমি উহা আদালতে দাং করলাম প্রদঃ ১: The PW 1 further added in his examination-in-chief“১নং বিবাদী আর্থিক ভাবে অস্বচ্ছল থাকার কারণে ১নং বিবাদী মূল্য পরিশোধে অপারগ হওয়ায় পিতার মাধ্যমে আমার নিকট নাঃ বাড়ী বিক্রয়ের প্রস্তাব দেয়৷ ১৫-১১-৮৪ তারিখে উক্ত প্রস্তাব দেয় । আমি প্রস্তাবে রাজী হই এবং আমাদের মধ্যে ১টি মৌখিক চুক্তি হয়। This PW 1 further added in his examination-in-chief the following evidence ১ম কিস্তির টাকা জমা দেয়ার পর সরকারের সাথে ১নং বিবাদীর নাঃ বাড়ী বিক্রয়ের চুক্তি হয় ১-৮-৮৫ তাং এই সেই কিক্রয় চুক্তি যা দাং করলাম প্রদঃ ২।”

17. From these evidence it is very much clear that the defendant No. 1 had no right to enter into any oral contract for sale of the suit house in favour of the PW 1 on 15-11-84 in view of the fact that the PW 1 himself admitted in his examination in chief that the suit house was an abandoned property on 15-11- 84. These evidence and the admission made by the PWI comes within the prohibition clause (h) of section 21 of the Specific Relief Act. The contract, if any, made by the defendant No. 1 dated 15-11-84 as stated in the plaint is a void contract and is not enforceable in law.

18. Furthermore, it is important to record that there is not a single piece of evidence available on record to show that there existed any contract between the plaintiffs and the defendant No. 1. The PW 1 is not the plaintiff in the suit. The PW 1 is the father of plaintiff No.2 and maternal uncle of plaintiff No. 1. The PW 1 did not adduce any evidence to substantiate the fact that any oral contract dated 15-11-84 was made between the plaintiffs and the defendant No. 1, the PW 1, PW 2 and the PW 7 adduced evidence to establish a verbal contract dated 15-11-84 between the defendant No. 1 and the PW 1, which is quite absurd to believe in view of the admitted fact that the defendant No. 1 did not acquire any right on 15-11-84 to enter into any verbal contract for sale of the suit house in favour of the plaintiffs. The PW 1 admitted the fact that the suit house being an abandoned house belonged to Government and it was allotted to the defendant No.1 and the defendant No.1 made payment of the first installment on 26-11-1984. The defendant No.1 entered into a contract for purchase of the suit house from the Government on 1-8-1985. So, the fact of oral contract as made out in the plaint fails totally and is hit by clause (h) of section 21 of the Specific, Relief Act.

19. Mr TH Khan, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party, submitted that the defendant No. 1 executed an agreement dated 23-8-1996 in favour of the plaintiffs agreeing upon to sell the suit house in their favour and that was executed pursuant to the oral agreement dated 15-11-84. That agreement was marked as Exhibit 4 and the learned Additional District Judge accepted the Exhibit 4 to be the subsequent development of oral contract dated 15-11-84 and decreed the suit.

20. Whether the Exhibit 4 bears any reference of any oral contract dated 15-11-84 and whether the suit could be decreed on relying upon the Exhibit 4 is a pertinent question in the suit and whether the learned Additional District Judge was justified in decreeing the suit on relying upon the Exhibit 4.

21. To meet this question let us see the contents of Exhibit 4 and the same is reproduced as under:

<u>22. On perusal of the Exhibit 4 it appears that there are two parts in the said agreement. In the first part, it appears that the father of the plaintiff No. 2 had paid the costs of the house to the Government and had paid the costs incurred towards registration of House No. 2-H/2-8 and the House No. 2-H/2-10 and the last part of the agreement shows that there happened a family arrangement between the defendants and the plaintiffs in respect of aforementioned 2 (two) houses. By that family arrangement the defendant undertook to register a family arrangement deed in favour of the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 in lieu of the House No. 2-H/2-8. There is no reference of any oral contract dated 15-11-84 in the said agreement. There is nothing to presume that there was a contract dated 15-11-1984 between the plaintiffs and the defendant No. 1 for sale of the suit property in their favour. The learned Additional District Judge without going through the contents of Exhibit-4 properly has held the said Exhibit 4 to be a deed of agreement pursuant to the oral contract dated 15-11-1984. There is no other evidence available on record to construe Exhibit 4 to be an agreement for sale of the suit house in favour of the plaintiffs following the alleged oral agreement dated 15-11-1984. The PW 7 being the mother of the PW 1 and the DW 1 simply admitted the fact that ১০ নং বাড়ী মজিবুর হারুণের (PW 1)  কাছে বিক্রয় করবে এমন কথা হয়েছিল। This Harunur Rashid is the father of the plaintiff No. 2. This Harunur Rashid is not a plaintiff in the suit. The learned Additional District Judge without properly considering the evidence of PW 7 has accepted the said evidence to be a positive evidence in support of the oral contract and decreed the suit. The Exhibit 4 cannot be accepted to be an agreement for sale of the suit house by the defendant No. 1 in favour of the plaintiffs. The PW 2 although deposed in support of oral contract dated 15-11-84 but his evidence will not help the plaintiff in any way in view of the fact that no title accrued in favour of the defendant No. 1 on 15-11-84 in the suit land and in view of clause (h) of section 21 of the Specific Relief Act. Admittedly, the defendant No. 1 has entered into a contract for purchase of the suit property from the Government on 1-8-1985. Admittedly, the defendant No.1 got the transfer deed executed and registered by the Mirpur Housing Society Authority on 15-9-1988. This being the admitted fact, it is absurd to believe that the plaintiffs entered into an oral contract with the defendant No.1 on 15-11-1984 to purchase the suit house before acquiring title by the defendant No.1. From the facts and circumstances and the discussion made above it is crystal clear like sunshine of broad daylight that the plaintiffs have hopelessly failed to prove oral contract. The learned Additional District Judge, Court No. 8, Dhaka has committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning a failure of justice on relying upon the Exhibit 4 and on relying upon the evidence of PW 7 and without considering the very admitted fact that no title accrued in favour of the defendant on 15-11-1984. Mr TH Khan, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties, referred to section 18 of the Specific Relief Act and submitted that this contract is valid in law. He also referred to a case law of Omar Ali Sheikh vs Shamsul Alarn reported in 55 DLR 257 in support of his contention. On perusal of the said decision, it appears that the defendant got the suit land from the Government on 28-11-78 and the suit for specific performance of contract was instituted in the year 1995. The trial Court decreed the suit and that decree was affirmed in appeal and the Rule issued in revision was discharged. A learned single Judge of this Division held that where a person having partial interest and subsequently acquired that interest, in that case the provision of section 43 of the. Transfer of Property Act applies and the transferee is entitled to get interest so acquired. The fact of the instant case is quite distinguishable from the facts of that case and that case law has got no manner of application in the instant case nor section 18 of the Specific Relief Act has got any manner of application in the instant case. The findings and decisions of the learned Additional District Judge is not sustainable in law and is liable to be set aside.</u>

23. Now, let us discuss the next point. Mr Yahiya, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submitted that the plaintiff No. 2 being a minor, the suit for specific performance of a contract is not maintainable and the trial Court lawfully dismissed the suit.

24. On perusal of the plaint and the evidence of PW 1, it appears that admittedly the plaintiff No. 2 is a minor. Mr TH Khan, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submitted that suit by a father on behalf of his minor son is maintainable. In the case-law of julhash Molla vs Ramani Kanta Malo and another reported in 47 DLR (AD) 35 that common question was raised. Our Appellate Division on relying upon the case law of Sarwarjan vs Fakhruddin Mahmud Chowdhury reported in ILR XXXIX Calcutta 232 (PC) held that a contract for the benefit of a minor is enforceable in law. Here, in the instant case, as we have already found that the plaintiffs have totally failed to prove any oral contract as stated in the plaint. So, the case law as cited above by learned Advocates of both the parties reported in 47 DLR (AD) 35 has got no manner of application in the instant case.

25. So far the question of limitation is concerned the Courts below did not give any finding upon the issue. The plaintiffs having failed to prove any existence of the contract as alleged in the plaint, I refrain myself from giving any finding upon the question of limitation.

26. From the facts and circumstances and the discussions made above, I hold that the plaintiffs have hopelessly failed to prove his alleged contract as stated in the plaint. The oral contract, if any, made on 15-11-1984 is also not tenable in law in view of the fact that on that date no title accrued in favour of the defendant No.1. That contract is void and not enforceable in law and is hit by clause (h) of section 21 of the Specific Relief Act. The judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Court No. 8, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 123 of 2002 is liable to be set aside. There is merit in the Rule.

26. In the result, the Rule is made absolute, however, without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree dated 27-4-2003 passed by the learned Additional District Judge in charge, Court No. 8, Dhaka, in Title Appeal No. 123 of 2002 allowing the appeal, decreeing the suit on reversing those dated 31-1-2002 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, in Title Suit No. 239 of 2001 is hereby set aside. The judgment and decree dated 31-1-2002 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, in Title Suit No. 239 of 2001 is hereby restored. The order of stay granted by this Court dated 15-6-2003 is hereby vacated.

The office is directed to send down the lower Court's records at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam, J: This Rule tinder section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure calls in question the judgment and decree dated 10.2.90 (decree signed on 15.2.1990) passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Habiganj in Title Appeal No. 77 of 1986 dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and decree dated 27.5.1986 (decree signed on 2.6.1986) passed by the learned Munsif, Habiganj Sadar in Tile Suit No. 106 of 1986.

2. The predecessor-in-interest of the petitioners late Abdur Razzak entered into a written agreement to purchase the suit property from late Habibullah predecessor-in-interest of the opposite parties. Both the original plaintiff and the defendant i.e. the predecessor of the present petitioners and the opposite parties No. 1-4 died during pendency of the suit and their legal heirs have been duly substituted as plaintiffs and defendants respectively.

3. The case of the plaintiffs-appellants-petitioners is that Syed Habibullah (now dead) proposed to sell the suit property for Taka 2,500/- to Abdur Razzak the predecessor-in-interest of the petitioners and executed a deed of agreement dated 2.7.65 and received taka 500/-in cash. It was stipulated that he would remove his thatched but from the contracted land and register the sale deed within 3 months on receipt of the balance consideration of taka 2000/-. Thereafter the said vendor did not register the said sale deed nor handed over possession of the suit land as agreed upon, over the above received from the purchaser Abdur Razzak balance consideration money in (eight) installments on various dates. The vendor Syed Habibullah also paid Taka 114/- to the purchaser for bringing patta. On 1.5.1968 the vendor refused to register the sale deed and hence the present suit was filed with a prayer for specific performance of contract and for getting possession of the suit land with compensation.

4. The defendants contested the suit by fling written statement contending, inter-alia, that the bainapatra is not correct. In fact the suit land has been mortgaged and the said document executed for mortgage by receiving Taka, 2,500/- the plaintiff. The suit land was khas land of the Government and the defendant did not get settlement of the said land at the time of execution of the bainapatra, so the question of sale did not arise at all. Later on 9.4.1968 the defendants got settlement. The loan amount was to be refunded with 10% interest. The plaintiff of back Taka 2,900 on 15.2.1968. Later on the defendant was asked to depose falsely in a case and when he refused enmity developed between the plaintiff and the defendant and the instant suit was filed. It is asserted by the defendant that there was no agreement for sale with the plaintiff. The plaintiffs suit wag false and vexatious.

5. The learned trial court on consideration of the materials on record dismissed the suit and being aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the trial court the present petitioners filed an appeal in the court of the learned District Judge, Habigonj which on transfer was heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, Habiganj. The learned Subordinate Judge by the impugned judgment and decree dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial court. The present petitioners then moved this court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and ob tamed the present Rule.

6. Mr. Shafiq Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiffs-appellants-petitioners submits that both the courts below harbored under misconception of law and taking an erroneous view of law and facts most illegally dismissed the suit. He further submits that bath the courts below failed to take notice of the provisions embodied in section 18(a) of the Specific Relief Act and thereby arrived at a wrong finding with regard to the deed of agreement exhibit 1. Mr. Shaftq Ahmed further submits that the earned trial Court in derogation of section 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act illegally allowed the defendants to adduce evidence to contradict the terms of the-written agreement exhibit 1. Mr. Shafiq Ahmed relying on the said sections of the Evidence Act submits that the finding of the learned vial Court to the effect that exhibit 1 in fact is not a deed of agreement but a deed of mortgage is absolutely erroneous and misconceived.

7. It appears that the nonce of the Rule was issued on the opposite parties in due course but none appears to oppose the Rule.

8. On a perusal of the judgment of the appellate court below it appears that he had dismissed the suit on the round that at the time of executing the agreement exhibit 1 the defendant had no right, the and interest in the suit land and the vendor subsequently in 1965 acquiced right, title and interest in the property. So the learned lower appellate court took the view that since the defendant had no subsisting interest in the suit property on 2.7.65 when the deed of agreement was executed, this did not confer any right to the plaintiff because the contract is void abinitto on the ground that the defendant at the relevant time had no vans ferable interest in tile suit land. The lower appellate court did not dismiss the appeal concurring with the finding of the trial court but dismissed the appeal on the sole ground that at the time of executing the deed of agreement the defendant had no interest in the suit land. The learned trial court, however, dismissed the suit on 3 other different grounds. The learned trial court found that there was a stipulation in the deed of agreement that the defendant would execute and register the necessary sale deed within 3 months from the date of execution of the agreement and it is an admitted fact that the defendant did not execute the necessary sale deed within stipulated period and even then the plaintiff paid balance consideration money to the defendant on different dates in 8 installments. The learned court took the view that the fact of payment of the part consideration money after expiry of the stipulated period of 3 months from the date of execution of the deed of agreement dated 2.7.65 exhibit 1 has lost its validity. It was no more enforceable contract in the eye of law. So the plaintiff had no right in law to enforce the contract against defendant. The second ground on which the learned trial court dismissed the suit is that exhibit Ka shows that the defendant had paid hack the consideration money with interest to the plaintiff. Relying on the oral evidence of the defendant in respect of the exhibit Ka the learned trial court arrived at a finding that exhibit 1, the alleged deed of agreement' is not in fact a deed of agreement but is a deed of mortgage as stated by the defendant. Since the defendant in terms of oral agreement repaid the capital along with interest the plaintiff had "0 subsisting interest to file the suit. The third ground on which the learned trial court relied upon is that the relief of the specific performance 'San equitable-relief and as such it is a discretion of the court as to whether it would exercise it in favour of the plaintiff or not. In a suit for specific performance of contract even if the plaintiff is able to prove his case he is not entitled to get the relief as prayed for automatically. In an appropriate case the court may award damage in lieu of specific performance of contract and for that proposition of law the learned court relies on a decision reported in 16 D.L.R, 239.

9. There is no denying of the fact and nobody in this ease dispute the fact that the relief of specific performance of contract is an equitable relief. It is also well settled proposition of law that in a suit for specific performance of contract the court is not bound to decree the suit by granting the prayer for specific performance of contract if in an appropriate case, a case of hardship is alleged and proved by, he defendant In the instant case the defect neither in his written statement nor in his de position has made out a case of hardship but the learned trial court making out a third case refused to decree the suit taking hardship as one of the grounds which in view of the fads and circumstances of the case is not justified in the instant case. The prayer of the plaintiff in the instant case cannot by an stretch of imagination he termed as unconscionable The law enunciated in 16 DIR. 239 10 disputed by anybody. That is a correct proposition of law which still holds the field hut he learned trial court wrongly relied on the decision which is not attracted in the present case and oil an erroncous view of law and facts refused to decree the suit.

10. I have already 'stated that Mr. Safiq Ahmed has relied on section 91 of the Evidence Act and submitted that the defendant was precluded in adducing any oral evidence the trial to contradict, very or to add to any terms of the deed of agreement dated 2.7.65 exhibit 1. The learned trial court failed to consider the implication of section 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act in the instant case and illegally allowed the defendant to adduce oral evidence to contradict and vary the terms of the deed of the plaintiff also failed to notice the same and did not raise any objection at the time of recording of the evidence by the learned trial Court. Be that as it may, the law is very much settled on this point. Section 91 lays down that when the terms and conditions of a contract or of a grant, or of any other disposition of property, have been set out in writing by agreement of the parties and in the case of all documents required by law to be in writing, the document is intended to he record of the transaction and therefore no other evidence shall be given to prove the transaction except the document it sell or secondary evidence thereof when such evidence is admissible.

11. Section 92 with some exception deals with the exclusion of extrinsic evidence to contradict, vary, add to subtract from the terms of such a document.

12. The Rule on which both the sections arc founded is that not only should the document embodying the terms of a contract, or grant between the parties he produced in proof of it but that the terms deliverately entered into and reduced to writing should not be allowed to be varied, contradicted, added to or subtracted from.

13. from a perusal of the judgment of the learned trial court I find that the learned trial court arrived at a positive uniting based on oral evidence adduced by the D.W.1 that the deed of agreement exhibit tin fact is not a deed of agreement for sale but is a deed of mortgage. In this connection it may also he mentioned that the exhibit 1 the deed of agreement is written by the defendant himself and he also admitted in his evidence before the learned trial court that he has executed exhibit. I voluntarily and does not dispute the contents of the deed of agreement of exhibit 1. Since it is a suit for specific performance of contract based on the deed of agreement for sale dated 2.7.65 the defendant in view of provisions of sections 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act ought not have been allowed to adduce any oral evidence to contradict .or subtract from the terms of the said agreement. The learned trial court miserably failed to consider this legal aspect of the case and on a misconception of Jaw and facts erroneously arrived at a finding that exhibit 1 is in. fact not a deed of agreement for sale but a deed of mortgage. In arriving at this finding the trial court heavily relied on exhibit Ka which is alleged by the defendant to be a money receipt acknowledging the repayment of the principal amount along with interest. The plaintiff categorically denied the execution of exhibit Ka. He in his evidence stated that the signature appear in exhibit Ka is not his, it is forged and fabricated one made by the defendant to dismiss his suit. This exhibit was sent to the Hand Writing Expert to obtain his opinion as to whether the signature appearing in this document is that of the plaintiff i.e. the predecessor in interest of the present petitioners. The Hand Writing Expert in view of paucity of materials before him tailed to give any positive opinion as to whether the signature appearing in exhibit 'Ka' is that of the plaintiff. Rut it appears from the record that he stated that the signature of the plaintiff does not tally with the specimen signature supplied to him for making comparison. The learned trial court on peculiar reasoning found that the signature appearing in exhibit 'Ka' is that of the plaintiff the learned trial court compared the signature appearing in exhibit 'Ka' with the signature of the plaintiff i.e. his signature in the plaint and vokalatnama of the suit as well arc his signature appearing in the deposition sheets. The learned trial court found that on two occasions the plaintiff signed his name in English and on the third occasion he signed his name in Bengali and this fact actuated the trial court to arrive at a finding that he did so with motive and the fact that on two occasions he signed in English and on one occasions he signed in Bengali indicate that the signature appearing ori exhibit `Ka' is genuine signature of the plaintiff. It is clear from the perusal of the judgment of the learned trial court that although the trial court compared the signature of the plaintiff with the normal signature of-the plaintiff appearing in the plaint and power as well as in the deposition sheets with the signature appearing on exhibit 'Ka" but there was no positive finding at all by the trial court that the signature ,appearing in exhibit. `Katally with the signature appearing in the plaint Vokalatnama and the deposition sheets. The trial court arrived at the conclusion that the signature appearing in exhibit 'Ka' is that of the plaintiff only on the ground that the plaintiff signed twice an English and once in Bengali in the plaint; vokalatnama and deposition sheet respectively. In that view of the fact it is also found that the learned trial court wrongly relied on exhibit 'Ka' and treated it as a genuine document.

14. I have already stated that the lower appellate court did not dismiss the appeal on the grounds as stated above but he dismissed the appeal on the ground that the defendant had no subsisting right, title or interest in the suit land on 2.7.65 when he entered into a deed of agreement with the plaintiff. So the agreement was void ab initio and it did not create any title in favour of the plaintiff and there remains nothing to enforce through the present suit. Mr. Shafiq Ahmed while making his argument before me relied on section 18(a) of the Specific Relief Act and submits that the learned Subordinate Judge failed to take notice of section 18(a) of the Specific Relief Act and taking an erroneous view of law had arrived at such a finding which is not tenable in law.

<u>15. Section 18(a) of the Specific Relief Act runs as follows: Where a person contracts to sell or let certain property, having only an imperfect title thereto, the purchaser or lessee has the following rights-</u>

<u>a) if the vendor or lessor has subsequently to the sale or lessee acquired any Interest in the property, the purchaser or lessee may compel him to make good the contract out of such interest."</u>

16. Here, may profitably refer to an analogous provision that exists in section 43 of the transfer of Property Act, 1882 which is as follows:

"Transfer by unauthorized person who subsequently acquires interest in property transferred:-

Where a person fraudulently or erroneously represents that he is authorized to transfer certain immoveable property and property to transfer such property for consideration, such transfer shall, at the option of the transferee operate on any interest which the transferor may acquire in such property at any time during which the contract of transfer subsists."

<u>17. The correct legal position is that if one enters into agreement to convey some property, in case, subsequent events should make it lawful, in equity he would be deemed to convey. When he after wards acquired the power. When a person enters into a contract without the power of performing that contract and subsequently acquires the power of performing that contract, he is found to do so. Thus, although an agreement to transfer the right of an heir apparent or spesis succession is invalid and enforceable 'under the law since it defeats the intention of the testator or is in fraud of parental authority, if an heir apparent or contingent remainder man conveys and estate absolutely to a purchaser for valuable consideration, and the estate expectant subsequently vests in the vendor, he would be held bound to make good the sale, and court would compel him to carry out his agreement and, make a legal conveyance, if necessary. For in such cases, the conveyance proving to be defective, the vendor could not ply that the contract had been already discharged by performance, and the interest, when it accused subsequently, would feed the grant by estoppel the legislature has adopted. The same principle in the case of contracts to sell or let property made by a .person, who has only an inspect title thereto. The purchaser or lesses in such a case, has the right, if the vendor or lessor has subsequently to the sale or lease acquired any interest in the property to compel him to make good the contract out of such interest. The section extends the principle sometimes referred to as feeding the grant by estoppel, which means where a party enters into a contract without, at the time, having the power of performance and subsequently ac quires that power, he becomes bound to make good the contract he had entered into.</u>

<u>18. Here we can also note that the expression imperfect title as appears in section 18(a) of the Specific Relief Act includes complete want, to title. In that view of the law even if it is conceded that at the time of entering into the agreement the defendant had no subsisting interest in the suit Land that cannot be a ground for refusing a decree of specific performance of contract. In the instant case admittedly in 1965 the defendant had acquired right, title and interest in the suit property. It is well settled that even if the vendor does not have a perfect title or no title at all at the time of entering into a contract for sale, he cannot avoid the contract in the future if the has subsequently acquired a right or interest in the property. In the present case admittedly the defendant was in possession of the suit land at the time of execution of the agreement for sale dated 2.7.65. So at the relevant time at least the defendant had some Interest in the property by way of possessory right and according to his own admission he acquired a perfect title of the suit land in 1965. In that view of the matter the defendant cannot come up with a defence in the present suit that he had no right, title and interest in the suit and at the relevant time. A court of law cannot allow a person to take advantage of his own fraud. Here in the instant case admittedly the defendant was in possession of the suit land at the relevant time of execution of sale agreement and he represented himself as the owner of the property and with that representation he had entered into the contract for sale vide exhibit 1 with the plaintiff. Since imperfect title includes complete want of title subsequent acquirement of right by the plaintiff in the suit land undoubtly entitled the plaintiff to get a decree for specific performance of contract. In the instant case it appears from the judgment of both the courts below that they have lost sight of section 18(a) of Specific Relief Act as well as section 43 of the Transfer of the Properly Act and ignoring those provisions of law most illegality arrived at a finding that the contract vide exhibit 1's void contract and the said finding cannot be sustained in law. In view of my aforesaid discussion I find substance in the submission made by the learned Advocate for the petitioners.</u>

19. In the result the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The judgment and decree dated 10.2.90 (decree signed on 15.2.90) passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Habiganj in Title Appeal No. 77 of 1986 and the judgment and decree dated 27.5.86 (decree signed on 2.6.86) passed by the learned Munsif. Habigonj Sadar in Title Suit No. 106 of 1986 are hereby set aside and the suit is decreed and the defendants are directed to register the necessary sale deed in favour of the plaintiffs within 2 months from the date of receipt of the record by the trial court failing which the plaintiffs will get the deed registered through court.

20. Send down the L.C. records to the Courts below at once.

End.
