full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the plaintiff-petitioners arises out of an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the impugned Judgment and order dated 31-1-2001 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Satkhira in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 35 of 2000 allowing the appeal on contest and vacating the order of temporary injunction granted on 24-5-2000 by the learned Assistant Judge, Thana Shyamnagar, Satkhira in Title Suit No. 63 of 1999.

2. The facts relevant for disposal of the Rule are that the plaintiff-petitioners instituted Title Suit No. 63 of 1999 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Thana Shyamnagar, Satkhira against the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 to 4 for declaration of title and enlistment of the suit land as vested property is illegal, collusive, ultra vires, fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiffs. The plaintiff-petitioners alleged, inter alia, that the suit land appertaining to SA Khatian No. 393 of Mouza Gabura, Police Station Shyamnagar area measuring 6.81½ decimals originally belonged to one Fazu Sarder and other co-sharer and out of that 4.37 acres of land is subject matter of the suit as described in "Ka" schedule of the plaint That Fazu Sarder died living behind 4 sons namely, Omar Ali Sarder, Gahar Ali, Sahar Ali and Anser Ali. The said successors and other co-sharer from 1966 onwards transferred their lands part by part to the predecessor of the plaintiffs and also plaintiff-petitioners vide different deeds of sale and by means of such transfer, the plaintiff-petitioners became the owners of the suit land and continued to enjoy the suit land by way of cultivation and residing in dwelling houses in some portion of the suit land by paying rents to the government for a long period but in spite of this the local Tahsildar, defendant No.4, threatened the plaintiffs on 10-6-1999 to disturb the peaceful possession of the suit land by giving Ejara of the suit land to the 3rd party treating as vested property and hence, the suit.

3. The plaintiffs after institution of the suit filed an application for temporary injunction under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 of the Civil Procedure Code against defendant opposite party Nos. 1-4 for restraining them from disturbing the peaceful possession of the plaintiff-petitioners by way of illegal and unlawful lease of the suit land to the 3rd party treating the suit land as vested property

4. The defendant-opposite party Nos. 1-4 contested the said application for temporary injunction by filing written objection denying all the material allegations of the petition and contending, inter alia, that one Narayan Chandra purchased 3.32 acres of suit land from original CS recorded tenants by 3(three) registered deeds and who having been in possession left this country for India in the year 1965 and in this manner the suit land was enlisted as vested property. The plaintiffs have had no title and possession in the suit land and they have no prima facie arguable case to get any order of temporary injunction in their favour and, as such, prayer for temporary injunction is liable to be rejected.

5. Both the parties filed number of documents and papers in support of their respective cases.

6. The learned Assistant Judge ultimately heard the matter and by an order of temporary injunction dated 24-5-2000 restrained the opposite party Nos. 1-4 from disturbing the peaceful possession of the plaintiffs by way of illegal and unlawful lease of the suit land till the disposal of the suit.

7. Being aggrieved by the order of temporary injection the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1-4 preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 35 of 2000 to the Court of learned District Judge, Satkhira against the said order and which was eventually heard by the learned Subordinate Judge 1st Court, Satkhira and who by his judgment and order dated 31-1-2001 allowed the appeal and vacated the order of temporary injunction dated 24-5-2000.

8. Mr AY Ahmed Ali, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that the learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in reversing order of temporary injunction of the trial Court without setting aside the material findings recorded by the learned Assistant Judge with reference to the deeds of sale and on assigning cogent reasons and the same has occasioned failure of justice. Mr Ahmed Ali further submits that the learned Court of Appeal below also ignored the material findings of the trial Court in respect of the documents filed by the plaintiffs, such as SA Khatian, 14 registered kabala deeds, yearly rent receipts, recent survey khatians and the plaintiffs' peaceful possession in the suit property and, as such, the impugned judgment of the lower Appellate Court is liable to be set aside. He finally, submits that admittedly the petitioners are in possession of the suit properties for over 25 years, since their purchase from the date of their vendors and they have been enjoying and possessing the same by payments of rents to the Government and, in such, situation the defendant Government could not dispossess them and on these consideration the trial Court rightly allowed the prayer for temporary injunction but the learned Court of Appeal below failed to apply his judicial mind in appreciating the plaintiff-petitioner's case from a correct angle and fell into error in deciding the prima facie case and balance of convenience and inconvenience of the parties and, as such, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside.

9. Mr Md Rabiul Alam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No.1, on the other hand, submits that the learned Court of appeal below, on proper consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and materials on record, was perfectly justified in reversing the order of temporary injunction of the trial Court on assigning sound reasons. He submits that one Narayan Chandra purchased 3.32 acres of suit land from original CS recorded tenants and who having been in possession left this country for India in the year, 1965 and in this manner the suit land was enlisted as vested property. Mr Chowdhury further submits that the so-called registered kabala deeds as filed by the plaintiffs are forged, collusive, fraudulent, concocted and created for the purpose to grab the suit land. Lastly, the learned Advocate, referring the impugned judgment and order, submits that the learned Court of appeal below rightly reversed the order of temporary injunction of the trial Court on the correct findings that the plaintiff's 4.37 acres of suit land in question is unspecified and they have failed to establish prima facie arguable case in their favour and hence there in no reasons to interfere with the impugned judgment and order of the learned subordinate judge.

10. Heard the learned Advocates of the both sides and perused the orders of the both Courts below and other connected papers.

<u>11. It appears from the order passed by the trial Court that after hearing the parties the trial Court found that the plaintiff-petitioners had a prima facie good arguable case on the ground that the plaintiffs filed a number of registered deeds, khatians, dakhilas and tax receipts, etc in respect of the suit land and which are important items of evidence of possession and thereby the learned Assistant Judge came to a finding that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land on the strength of documents, such as registered deeds, khatians, dakhilas and tax receipts, etc. The trial Court also found that the Government defendant could not or did not file any document that one Narayan Chandra purchased 3.32 acres of suit land from CS recorded tenants and who left this country for India in 1965 and thereon the suit land was enlisted as vested property.</u>

12. The lower appellate Court, in its turn, on consideration of the materials found on record that the registered kabala deeds as filed by the plaintiffs are forged, collusive, fraudulent, concocted and created for the purpose to grab the suit land and the plaintiff's 4.37 acres of suit land is unspecified and they failed to establish prima facie arguable case in their favour but the learned Assistant Judge without considering these aspects came to an erroneous decision and granted temporary injunction as sought for.

13. Upon a careful scrutiny it appears that the suit filed by the plaintiff-petitioners is a suit for declaration of title and enlistment of the suit land as vested property is illegal, collusive, fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiffs. The plaintiff's title is based upon a valid purchase of the property by a number of duly registered deeds since 1966-1981. On the contrary, the defendant No.1 contended that the suit land in question appeared to have been held as vested property and the said purchased deeds of the plaintiffs are forged and concocted. But it appears that the Government-defendant could not proceed to claim in such property by way of an appropriate suit for declaration of title and cancellation of the petitioner's registered deeds.

14. In the foregoing facts and circumstances of the case and in absence of proper trial, it is very difficult to agree with the contention raised by the defendants to the effect that the plaintiffs have no right, title and possession in the suit land. Therefore, in such a situation, I find that the findings of the trial Court are well founded that the plaintiff-petitioners have been able to prove their prima facie title and possession in the suit land. The petitioners have filed the instant suit praying for declaration of their title and enlistment of the suit land as vested property is illegal, collusive, ultra vires, fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiffs and also prayed for temporary injunction under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 of the Civil Procedure Code against defendant-opposite party Nos. 1-4 for restraining them from disturbing the peaceful possession of the plaintiff-petitioners by way of illegal and unlawful lease of the suit land to the 3rd party treating the suit land as vested property and, as such, if they are allowed to be evicted form the suit land they will suffer irreparable loss and injury and, on the contrary, since the defendants are out of possession they will not suffer any loss or injury. Balance of convenience and inconvenience, it appears to me, is also in favour of the plaintiff-petitioners. I, therefore, find substance and force in the submission of the learned Advocate Mr AY Ahmed Ali appearing on behalf of the petitioners. The learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in reversing the order of the trial Court without reversing material finding arrived at by the trial Court on consideration of the evidence on record regarding the principles governing for granting temporary injunction, namely, the balance of convenience and inconvenience and the question of irreparable loss and injury. Moreso, the appellate Court as final Court of fact did not give any independent finding by assigning cogent reasons that the plaintiffs have no tittle and possession of the suit land.

<u>15. For the reasons stated above, I hold that the plaintiffs-petitioners have been able to establish a good prima facie arguable case inasmuch as they have filed a number of documents and papers in support of their claim, such as 14 registered deeds, khatians, dakhilas and tax receipts, etc and thus, therefore, the well-established principles of law governing the grant of temporary injunction are 1) the plaintiff has to establish a good prima facie case 2) it has to be shown that the plaintiff will suffer irreparable loss, if the injunction prayed for is not granted and 3) the balance of convenience and inconvenience lies in favour of the plaintiff and in favour of granting the temporary injunction prayed for, are attracted in its entirety in this case. Therefore, on that score the learned subordinate judge erred in law in reversing the order of temporary injunction passed by the learned trial Court and the same has resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. However, here it may be mentioned that Mr AY Ahmed Ali, the Advocate, at the end of the day frankly submits that he will have no objection, if the order of temporary injunction be modified by substituting it with an order for maintaining status quo pending disposal of the suit which will also serve the interest of the plaintiff-petitioners.</u>

<u>16. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order dated 31-1-2001 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Satkhira in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 35 of 2000 is hereby set aside. The order of status quo granted by this Court at the time of issuance of the Rule shall continue till disposal of the suit.</u>

17. The suit is an old one of 1999, as such, the learned Assistant Judge, Thana Shyamnagar, Satkhira is directed to dispose of the Title Suit No. 63 of 1999 as expeditiously as possible, preferably within six months from the date of receipt of this Judgment.

Communicate the judgment to the learned Assistant Judge, Thana Shyamnagar, Satkhira immediately.

End.

full_judgment:
Abu Sayeed Ahammed, J: This Rule at the instance of plaintiffs against the judgment and decree dated 25.1.93 passed by Sub-ordinate Barisal in Title Appeal No. 248 of 1989 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 30.8.89 passed in Title Suit 195 of 1985 by the Senior Assistant Judge, Barisal decreeing the suit setting aside an ex-parte decree.

2. Plaintiff's case in short, is that predecessor-in-interest of plaintiffs and of defendants named Aynuddin Howlader purchased the suit property at his own money and was in possession after mutating his name in Mutation Case 21KT/445C.M, 57-58. On 02 acres land of suit plot No.1145 Aynuddin constructed a mosque and made it as waqf property by a registered deed of waqf on 9.7.58. In the said deed defendant 2 son of Aynuddin is an attesting witness. Further case of the plaintiff is that the suit property wrongly and illegally was listed as vested property in vested property case 301 of 1970. On 27.1.79 Aynuddin himself made an application for release of the said property. The application having not been fruitful Aynuddin again made another application on 6.5.81 and his son defendant 3 in that application attested thump impression of Aynuddin as for his old age he could not put signature at that time. The property was released from the abandoned property list by order dated 11.5.83 in favour of Aynuddin. Aynuddin thereafter died. Plaintiffs include 2nd wife of Aynuddin and her sons and daughters. The defendants include 1st wife and sons and daughters of first wife of Aynuddin. Plaintiffs and defendants inherited the suit property jointly and plaintiffs, share is 6 annas 18 gondas 17 tils. The plaintiffs are in possession of the same. They came to learn on 28.2.85 that an ex-parte aecree was obtained by defendants in Title Suit 411 of 1974 in the 6th Court of Munsif, Barisal on 19.7.75, keeping Aynuddin in darkness about proceedings of suit by suppressing summons from Aynuddin and practising fraud upon the Court and hence petitioners have brought the instant suit for setting aside the said ex-parte decree on the ground of fraud practised upon Aynuddin Howlader and the Court.

3. The defendants 1 and 2 contested the suit by filling a written statement in denial of the allegations of the plaint. Their case is that the suit land did not belong to Aynuddin Howlader. It belonged to defendants 1-5 who had acquired the same by purchases in 1955 from its previous owners Khitish Chandra and two others at their own money and allegations of suppression of summons from Aynuddin is false.

4. The trial court decreed the suit and set aside ex-parte decree. Against the same defendants took appeal. The plaintiffs contested. The appeal was allowed and the judgment and decree of the trial court have been set aside and suit was dismissed. Appellate court found that the suit is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and as such not maintainable. Against the same the plaintiffs have obtained this Rule.

5. Mr. Quayum learned Advocate for petitioners submits that the suit is embraced within the provision of section 146 of the Code of Civil Procedure which reads as follows:-

"Proceedings by or representatives. Save as otherwise provided by this Code or by any law for the time being in force. Where any proceeding may be taken of application made by or against any person then the proceedings may be taken or the application may be made by or against any person claiming under him".

6. According to him the present plaintiffs being hens of Aynuddin they can maintain the suit very well and he persuades me to go through the finding of the appellate court as follows :-

“স্বীকৃত মতে যেহেতু পক্ষগন আইনুদ্দীনের ওয়ারিশ সেহেতু বাদীপক্ষ কোন ক্রমেই বাটোয়ারা ডিক্রির প্রার্থনা ছাড়া বর্ণিত আকারের প্রার্থনার প্রতিকার পাইতে পারে না। প্রকৃত পক্ষে বাদী পক্ষের উচিত চিল সুনিদিষ্ট প্রতিকার আইনের ৪২ ধারার বিধানে বিরোধীয় ডিক্রি চ্যালেজ্ঞসহ আইনুদ্দীনের ওয়ারিশ হিসাবে প্রাপ্ত অংশের ডিক্রি প্রার্থনার মামলা করা।

<u>7. It is well settled that against the ex-parte decree four kinds of reliefs are available to an aggrieved party those are (1) Miscellaneous case under Order 9, Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, (2) an appeal, (3) a review under Order 47 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure and (4) A separate suit can be filed for setting aside the ex-parte decree. It has been decided in the case of Md. Wasiq Khan V. Md. Sabiq Khan and others, reported in 31 DLR(AD) 51 that when anybody suffers from an ex-parte decree he can maintain a suit for setting aside the same.</u>

8. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed on the other hand submits that for setting aside an ex-parte decree the suit must be filed as provided under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act which reads as follows:-

"42-Discretion of Court as to declaration of status of right; Any person entitled to any legal character or to any right as to any property, may institute a suit against any person denying or interested to deny his title to such- character or right, and the Court may in its discreation make therein a declaration that he is so entitled, and the plaintiff need not in such ask for any further relief. Provided that no Court shall make any such declaration where the plaintiff, being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title, omits to do so".

9. In view of the above legal position Mr. Ahmed Submits that the appellate court has decided the issue, namely, the maintainability of the suit legally and rightly he has dismissed the suit. In reply to the same Mr. Quayum submits that though the suit does not come within the ambit of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act strictly as it is a suit for setting aside the exparte decree but it is embraced by the provision of section 9 and 146 of the Code of Civil Procedure, provision of section 9 of the Code reads as follows:-

"Courts to try all Civil suits unless barred. The Courts shall (subject to the provisions herein contained) have jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature excepting suits of which their cognizance is whether expressly or impliedly barred."

10. My considered view is that the present suit is maintainable under Sections 9 and 146 of the Code of Civil procedure and also not strictly barred by principle of Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, as I find that the plaintiffs are co-sharers of the defendants as it has found place in the judgment of the appellate Court.

The appellate Court also found that since sufficient court fee has not been paid for setting aside the decree the suit is not maintainable, Section 7 viii(A) has been added by way of amendment to the Court Fees act (East Bengal, Act XIII if 1950) wherein it has been provided as follows :-

"7.viii(A) to set aside decrees: In suits to set aside decrees passed for ascertained amounts-according to the amounts of the decrees sought to be set aside, or where such decrees are not for any ascertained amounts the fee payable shall be the same as paid on the plaints of the suits in which the questioned decrees were passed'.

In the operative portion of the appellate court judgment it has found that the court fee was sufficient.

11. In view of the aforesaid provision of law I hold that the Court fee was sufficient in filing the instant suit and as such finding of the appellate court is faulty. It appears that in Mutation Case No. 21KT/445C.M. of 1957-58 the suit property was mutated in the name of Aynuddin. Defendants failed to prove that the suit property was acquired by their money. Their case is that they purchased the property by the money they had obtained in their Akika ceremony and marriage ceremony, but their witnesses totally failed to prove the same. It is also on record as oral evidence, that at the time of purchasing suit property the defendants concerned were unmarried. Finding of trial court in this respect has not been controverted by the appellate court. It is also not denied that Aynuddin erected a mosque on .02 decimal of land of Dag. No.1145 and on 9.7.58 he made a deed of Waqf in favour of the mosque. Defendant 3 a son of Aynuddin Howlader was an attesting witness in the Waqf deed. In the application filed on 6.5.81 by Aynuddin himself for release of the suit property from list of vested property defendant 3 attested the thump impression of Aynuddin. The plaintiffs of the present suit are admittedly the second wife and issues of her by Aynuddin. He married his 2nd wife before purchase of the disputed property. It is also on record as oral evidence that the plaintiffs are in possession of a portion of the suit property which has been found by the trial court and could not be destroyed by counter evidence. I hold that these facts also support maintainability of suit.

12. Another very important aspect is that in the plaint the address of Aynuddin Howlader, in Title Suit 411 of 1974, was written as follows:-

“আইনুদ্দিন হাওলাদার পিতা মৃত সফেজুদ্দিন হাওলাদার সাকিনচর বুখাই নগর ষ্টেশন কোতয়ালী হাং সাং বরিশাল কাউনিয়া রোড ষ্টেশন কোতয়ালী বরিশাল।”

<u>13. According to plaint Aynuddin Howlader was residing at the time of institution of the suit at Barisal Town. But it appears from the service return of the summons that the process-server went to his village address and on tender of the summons purportedly to Aynuddin the same having been refused it was served by hanging. On the basis of that very tainted service of summons the ex-parte dectee was passed against Aynuddin taking away the right of the plaintiffs from the suit property. Therefore my considered view is that the ex-parte decree definitely suffers from fraud which is apparent from the service of return of summons itself. The learned Appellate Court has not decided this point as he confined himself on the point of maintainability of the suit; For non-discussion by the Appellate Court about service of summons upon Aynuddin reason has been given that since no specific issue has been framed on that point discussion is not warranted. My opinion is that when there were allegations in the plaint and in view of issue No.3 the same could be discussed by the appellate court as principal claim of the appellant is that the decree was vitiated by ground for non-service of summons upon defendant Aynuddin.</u>

14. It is admitted by Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned counsel for opposite parties that the present plaintiffs being heirs of said Aynuddin Howlader whatever reliefs Aynuddin Howlader could have prayer, the present plaintiffs also can pray the same. His pin point argument is that in the suit declaration of title having not been prayed although the plaintiffs are heirs of Aynuddin Howlader, it is not maintainable and he relies on the decision of 6 BCR(AD)56.

15. Mr. Quayum, for petitioners submits that in view of the facts and circumstances of the present case, specially for the admitted position that the plaintiffs are heirs of Aynuddin visa-vis-co-sharers of the defendant this case is distinguishable from the case of the 6 BCR(AD)56. (Munsur Ali Mallik V. Md. Nurul Haque Mallik and others).

16. I have gone through the judgment of both the courts below and also heard the learned Advocates of both the sides to a reasonable length and also meticulously read the said decision of our Appellate Division I accept the submission of Mr. Quayum that the present case is distinguishable as I find title of the plaintiffs have still rooted in the suit property and the plaintiffs therefore can maintain their present suit, (Keramat Ali Vs. Ramizuddin Ahmed, 39 DLR 334). Therefore in view of the facts and circumstances of the present case, the principle enuntiated in the case of 6 BCR(AD)56 not applicable in the instant case. Appellate court itself found the plaintiff as co-sharer of the defendants and it is not said that the plaintiffs are not in possession. It has been held in 27 DLR (AD) 143 that possession of one co-sharer is possession of all co-sharers. So, in my view the instant suit is maintainable as it is clear from the evidence that the plaintiffs are not out of possession of the suit property. The effect of setting aside the ex-parte decree is in reality revival of the original suit.

17.Regard being had to the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record both oral and documentary I am of the view that the appellate court committed illegality resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice and therefore the impugned judgment and decree of the appellate Court is liable to be set aside and the title suit 421 of 1974 shall revive and proceed with its trial (Dharanidhar Aditya and others Vs. Hamagu Chandra Geina and others 21 CWN 1087).

18. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs.

19. The judgment and decree of the appellate Court are set aside and those of the trial Court's are affirmed. Ex-parte judgment and decree passed in title suit 411 of 1974 on 19.7.75, are set aside the said suit is restored and revived and the plaintiffs of the present suit shall be allowed to be substituted as defendants and they shall be allowed to contest the suit on merits, by filing new written statements and adducing evidence if so desire. The trial court shall decide the suit on merits as shortly as possible.

20. No order as to costs. The lower court's record shall be sent down at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Farid Ahmed J: The Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-3 to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 26-2-2012 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Cox's Bazar in Other Class Suit No. 4 of 2010 rejecting the application filed by the petitioner under Order VII, rule 11(d) read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure should not be set aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to the court may seem fit and proper.

2. The opposite party Nos. 1-3 as plaintiffs on 21-1-2010 instituted other class suit No. of 2010 in the 151 Court of Joint District Judge, Cox's Bazar against the petitioners and opposite party Nos. 4-24 for declaration of title and confirmation of possession in respect of the land described in the schedule to the plaint and for further declaration that the decree 86 passed by the then Munsif, Cox's Bazar in Other Class Suit No. 235 of 1972 is void and inoperative.

3. In that suit defendant-petitioners filed an application under, Order VII, rule 11(d) read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure alleging that the predecessors of the defendant Nos. 1-3 had instituted the Other Class Suit No. 235 of 1972 before the then Munsif, Cox's Bazar impleading the predecessor of the defendant No. 4 and others as defendants for declaration of their title on the self-same land and for khas possession. The said suit was decreed on contest on 31-7-1986 and that the predecessor of the present defendant No. 4 and others had filed Other Appeal No. 144 of 1986 in the Court of learned District Judge who after hearing by judgment and decree dated 4-5-1987 allowed the appeal and thereby set aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. Thereafter defendant-petitioners and their predecessor filed Civil Revision No. 562 of the 1987 before the High Court Division and upon contested hearing the Rule was made absolute and the Title Suit No. 235 of 1972 was decreed. The predecessor of the present plaintiff-opposite parties long after 6 years filed civil petition for Leave to Appeal No. 870 of 2009 before the Appellate Division who after hearing by judgment and order dated 12-11-2009 dismissed the civil Petition, thus the present suit is barred by principle of res-judicata.

4. The plaintiff-opposite parties filed written objection against the application for rejection of plaint.

5. The learned Judge by the impugned order No. 23 dated 26-2-2012 rejected the said application for rejection of plaint on the finding that without examining the witnesses at the time of hearing of the suit the point raised by the petitioners cannot be decided and that there is no lawful reason for rejection of the plaint.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said order of the Joint District Judge, the defendant-petitioners moved this Court and obtained the present rule.

7. Mr Dulal Mallick, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of defendant-petitioners has submitted that the predecessor of the present petitioners instituted Title Suit No. 235 of 1972 against the predecessor of the present plaintiff-opposite parties for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession and the said suit went upto the Appellate Division which affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court decreeing the suit and, as such, the present suit for the self-same suit land between the same parties are barred by the principle of res-judicata. He thereafter has submitted that from the judgment decree of the previous suit it would appear that predecessor of the present petitioners obtained decree declaring title and recovery of khas possession over the self-same property and thus, if the plaint cannot be rejected under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil procedure, the Court has ample power to reject the same under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure as the proceeding of the present suit will be a fruitless litigation. In support of his submission he referred the case of Abdul Jalil vs Islamic Bank Bangladesh Ltd reported in 53 DLR (AD) 12 and the case of Rasheda Begum vs MM Nurussafa reported in 24 BLD (AD) 223 = 9 BLC (AD) 223.

8. On the other hand Mr Omar Farook, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of plaintiff-opposite parties has submitted that the question of res-judicata cannot be agitated by filing an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, thus the learned Joint District Judge rightly rejected the application. In support of his submission he referred the case of Mahbubul Haque (Md) vs Md A Kader Munshi reported in 52 DLR (AD) 49 and the case of Sreemati Pushpa Rani Das vs AKM Habibur Rahman reported in 13 BLD (AD) 217. He also has submitted that in disposing of an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil procedure the Court cannot consider any point beyond the pleadings. He thereafter has submitted that there is no ingredients of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the application for rejection of plaint, in such circumstances the learned Joint District Judge has not committed any illegality in rejecting the application for rejection of plaint.

9. The petitioners have annexed the plaint of the present Title Suit No. 4 of 2010 and the previous judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 235 of 1972 of the Court of the then Munsif, Cox's Bazar. Ongoing through the decree passed in previous Title Suit No. 235 of 1972 it appears that the heirs of plaintiffs of the previous title suit have been impleaded as decree-holder defendants and other defendants of the previous title suit have been impleaded as 2nd party defendants in the present suit.

10. According to plaintiff-opposite parties, they purchased the suit property from the defendants of the previous title suit. The schedule of present Other Class Suit No. 4 of 2010 is as under:

Mouza-Zilongja, Upazila and District -Cox's Bazar, RS Khatian No. 526, MRR Khatian No. 552, RS Plot No. 2323 area of land 12½ decimal situated on the Western side of the suit plot corresponding to BS, Khatian No. 1367, plot No. 6561.

11. The schedule of previous Other Class Suit No. 235 of 1972 is as under:

Mouza-Zilongja, Upazila and District -Cox's Bazar, RS Khatian No. 526, MRR Khatian No. 552, RS Plot No. 2323 area .30 decimal of land situated on the Western side of the suit plot.

12. The judgment and order passed by the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 870 of 2009, the judgment and order dated 18-1-2004 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 562 of 1987 and the judgment and decree passed in other Class Suit No. 235 of 1972 have been annexed with the revisional application as annexure-D series.

13. In Paragraph 4 of the Title Suit No. 1 of 2010 plaintiff-opposite parties claimed that they purchased the suit land in 2009 from the heirs of defendants of previous Title Suit No. 235 of 1972. In that title suit plaintiffs vendors had lost their title upto Appellate Division. In the present suit their claim over the self-same property was the subject matter of the previous Title Suit No. 235 of 1972.

14. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite parties cited two decisions. In the case of Sreemati Pushpa Rani Das vs AKM Habibur Rahman reported in 13 BLD (AD) 217 their lordships held that the plaint, cannot be rejected only on point of res-judicata through an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In that case the plaintiffs withdrew their previous Title Suit No. 78 of 1977 for declaration of title and thereafter instituted another Title Suit being No. 58 of 1991. In the same Court defendant filed Title Suit No. 93 of 1990 for permanent injunction and got decree on contest. Against the said decree the respondent filed Title Appeal No. 100 of 1991. The defendant pleaded that the Title Suit No. 58 of 1991 was barred by res-judicata in that circumstances, the Appellate Division held that the same is not barred by res-judicata.

15. In the case reported in 52 DLR (AD) 49 the plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 17 of 1998 for cancellation of a previous decree on the ground that his predecessor was neither a party in the previous Money Suit No. 5 of 1932 nor the suit property was auction sold in Money Execution Case No. 14 of 1933 and thus the defendants practiced fraud upon the plaintiff as well as the Court by withholding some documents and, as such, the plaintiff was deprived of the opportunity to verify the correctness of the same by taking back the impugned documents and plaintiff came to know about the forged nature of the aforesaid documents by obtaining certified copy of the suit register relating to the aforesaid Money Suit No. 5 of 1932. In that circumstances the Court held that the suit was not barred by res-judicata.

16. From the above facts we find that the above two decisions are not at all applicable in the fact and circumstance of the present case. It is true that a plaint of a suit should not be rejected under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure only on point of res-judicata. But the fact of the present case is quite different. Apparently it shows that the predecessor of the plaintiff-opposite parties lost their title upto Appellate Division and after settling dispute finally by the Appellate Division the present plaintiff-opposite parties purchased some lands in 2009 from the predecessor of the defendants of the former suit and they instituted present suit for declaration of title, confirmation of possession and for further declaration that the decree, passed in previous Title Suit No. 235 of 1972 against the predecessor of the present plaintiffs are void and not binding upon them. The issue of present title suit was decided by the Court finally in previously instituted suit and that issue cannot be agitated in the subsequent suit.

17. In the case of Rasheda Begum vs MM Rurussafa reported in 24 BLD (AD) 223 = 9 BLC (AD) 223 referred by the defendant-petitioners. Their lordships of the Appellate Division held that:

"…….. rejection of plaint is not confined to the provision of Order XI, rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In a fit or appropriate case i.e. while the proceeding initial is an abuse of the process of the court or a contrive to achieve something which the party failed upon proceeding under the law provided for or any other case akin to cases as mentioned above the Court taking recourse of the provision of section 151 would be competent to reject the plaint or strike out part of the relief prayed for or sought in a subsequent suit...."

18. The learned Advocate for the petitioners further has referred the case of Abdul Jalil vs Islamic Bank Bangladesh Ltd. reported in 53 DLR (AD) 12. In that case also it has been decided that:

"It is well settled that where a plaint cannot be rejected under Order. VII, rule 11 Code of Civil Procedure the court may invoke its inherent jurisdiction and reject the plaint taking recourse to section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure"

19. These two cases referred on behalf of petitioners are applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case. The plaintiff-opposite parties purchased the suit property in 2009 through the persons who lost their title upto Appellate Division. In such circumstances, we find that the proceeding of the present suit between the same parties is nothing but futile exercise.

20. In paragraph No. 6 of the plaint of present Title Suit No. 4 of 2010 the plaintiff-petitioners has stated that on obtaining the certified copy of the judgment and decree passed in Other Class Suit No. 235 of 1972 they came to know about the decree passed in previous suit. In prayer Kha of the present title suit they prayed under:

“খ) কক্সবাজার মুনসেফী আদালতের অপর ২৩৫/৭২ ইং নম্বর মামলার ৩১-৭-৮৬ইং তারিখের রায় ডিক্রী (ডিক্রী স্বাক্ষরিত ৬-৯-৮৬ইং) রহিত করিবার পক্ষে ডিক্রী প্রচার করিবার”

<u>21. Ongoing through the plaint of the present suit it also appears that the present plaintiff-opposite parties knowing fully well about the previous title suit and proceeding of the said suit upto Appellate Division and losing of title of their predecessor upto that stage, instituted the present suit which is nothing but futile exercise. In such circumstances, we find merit in this rule.</u>

<u>In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The judgment and order dated 26-2-2012 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Court, Cox's Bazar in Other Class Suit No. 4 of 2010 is hereby set aside and the plaint of Title Suit No. 4 of 2010 is rejected.</u>

End.

full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman, J: This appeal at the instance of the plaintiff-appellants is directed against the judgment and order dated 14.6.87 passed by a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division, Rangpur Session, in Civil Revision No. 72 of 1986 discharging the Rule, thereby staying execution proceeding arising out of the decree passed in Other Suit No. 730 of 1984 of the Court of Munsif, Sadallahpur.

2. The short fact relevant for disposal of the appeal is that the appellants and their mother Gulsan Bewa, as plaintiffs, filed Other Suit No. 19 of 1963 for partition of the suit land against Banisuddin, lather of respondent No. 1 and others in the Second Court of Munsif at Gaibandha. On transfer to the First Court of Munsif at Gaibandha the said suit was renumbered as Other Suit No. 83 of 1964 (finally renumbered as Suit No. 730 of 1984 of the Court of Munsif, Sadallahpur). In that suit a contested decree was passed on 31.8.68 in preliminary from. Thereafter Banisuddin and other defendants preferred Other Appeal No. 254 of 1968 before the District Judge, Rangpur and the same was dismissed on 10.4.72 by the Subordinate Judge, Rangpur. After decision in the aforesaid appeal, Banizuddin, father of respondent No. 1 died and the heirs of Banizuddin including his son respondent No. 1 preferred Second Appeal No. 148 of 1973. In the Memorandum of Second Appeal, respondent No. 1 appeared as major, appellant No. 6, and respondent No. 1 as major signed the Vokalatnama, During the pendency of the aforesaid Second Appeal the appellants filed an application before the First Court of Munsif at Gaibandha for drawing up of the final decree in Other Suit No. 83 of 1964. At that time respondent No. 1 and other defendants filed application for time to bring stay order from the High Court Division, Subsequently respondent No. 1 obtained an interim stay order and the further proceeding in O.C. Suit No. 83 of 1964 was stayed the said Rule was, however, discharged for non-prosecution on 30.1.78. The Second Appeal No. 148 of 1973 was finally heard and dismissed on 18.10.82. The decree passed in the Second Appeal shows respondent No. 1 as a major. The appellants then filed another application before the learned Munsif for drawing up of final decree in Other Suit No. 83 of 1964. This Other Suit No. 83 of 1964 was again transferred and renumbered as Other Suit No. 730 of 1984 of the Court of Munsif, Sadullahpur Upazila. In order to prevent passing of final decree in Other Suit No. 730 of 1984, respondent No. 1 filed a suit being Other Suit No. 734 of 1984 in the Court of Munsif Sadullahpur Upazila for setting aside the preliminary decree passed in Other Suit No. 83 of 1964 on the ground that respondent No. 1 was fraudulently shown as a major defendant in the suit though he was minor and as such the decree was void. After filing Suit No. 734 of 1984, respondent No. 1 filed an application in Other Suit No. 730 of 1984 for stay of the proceedings (for drawing up of final decree) of the said suit till the disposal of Other Suit No. 734 of 1984. The learned Munsif of Sadullahpur Upazila after hearing of the parties by order dated 24.12.84 stayed all further proceeding in Other Suit No. 730 of 1984 till the disposal of Other Suit No. 734 of 1984. Being aggrieved by the said order dated 24.12.84, the appellants and their mother, Guljan Bewa filed Civil Revision No. 72 of 1985 and obtained a Rule and the same was discharged by a single Judge of the High Court Division on 14.6.87 on the finding that the execution proceeding arising out of the decree passed in Other Suit No. 730 of 1984 should be stayed as the question of minority of respondent No. 1 will be decided in Other Suit No. 734 of 1984.

3. Leave was granted to consider whether the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division was correct in granting stay in the execution proceeding arising out of the decree passed in Other Suit No. 730 of 1984 by overlooking the material facts that Mosleuddin, respondent No. 1, described himself as major in his Vokalatnama dated 17th July, 1972 and in the Memorandum of Appeal filed in the Second Appeal and that the said Mosleuddin was never impleaded as a party in the original partition suit and on the contrary his father was impleaded as a party in the suit and as such the question of setting aside the preliminary decree on the ground of Moslemuddin being impleaded as a minor in the original suit does not arise and on this false, frivolous and untenable ground the drawing up of tlit5 final decree on the basis of the decision in the Second Appeal cannot be stayed.

<u>4. It appears from the materials on record that original Suit No. 83 of 1964 (renumbered as Suit No. 730 of 1984) Moslemuddin (respondent No. 1) was not a party in the suit and his father Banizuddin was a defendant. After passing of the decree, the appeal that was preferred before the lower appellate court was also filed by respondent No. l’s father Banizuddin. The Second Appeal was filed by respondent No. 1 describing himself as a major along with other heirs of Banizuddin. The Vokalatnama was also signed by Moslemuddin in the Second Appeal showing him as a major. It appears from the record that after the dismissal of the second appeal on 18.10.82, the appellant filed an application for drawing up of the final decree in the original suit. Subsequent thereto respondent No. 1 tiled Other Suit No. 734 of 1984 raising the question of his minority in the suit and voidability of the decree on that ground. The learned Single Judge while disposing of the revision failed to consider the above facts and without application of judicial mind on the materials on record wrongly held that in Other Suit No. 734 of 1984 the question as to whether Moslemuddin was a major or minor will be decided and on that score he wrongly stayed the execution proceeding arising out of the decree passed in Other Suit No. 730 of 1984. The original suit was decreed in preliminary from in 1984, and by passing this stay order the drawing up of the final decree passed in a suit filed 25 years back was illegally and arbitrarily stayed. It may be stated here that granting of stay is a discretionary matter of the court, but in the facts and circumstances of the present case the materials on record were not considered and on a total non-consideration of the materials on record the execution proceeding in the Other Suit No. 730 of 1984 was stayed. The learned Single Judge on this false and frivolous plea as to the minority of respondent No. 1 illegally granted stay order. Further, the second appeal having been tiled by respondent No. 1 showing as major there cannot be any question of fraud on the part of the appellants in obtaining the decree in the original suit and as such the execution of the decree has been improperly stayed in this case.</u>

5. Accordingly, the impugned judgment of the High Court Division is set aside and the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Naimuddin Ahmed, J: This revisional application is directed against the judgment and order passed by the District Judge, Jamalpur, in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 8 of 1984 on 16.9.85 whereby he affirmed the judgment and order passed by the Subordinate Judge, Sherpur, in Miscellaneous Case No. 14 of 1982 whereby he dismissed the application under Rule 13 of Order 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex-parte decree in Other Class Suit No. 33 of 1978 disposed of by him on 28.12.1983.

2. The facts are that the opposite parties instituted Other Class Suit No. 33 of 1978 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Sherpur and in this suit the present petitioner was the defendant. The suit was decreed ex-parte on 5.5.79 in absence of the petitioner. She then tiled an application under Rule 13 of Order 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex-parte decree on the ground that no summons was served on her and she came to know about the exparte decree on 30.5.82 and this application was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 14 of 1982. The opposite parties resisted the Miscellaneous case contending that the summons was duly served on the petitioner and that the application was barred by limitation as she had failed to apply for setting aside the ex-parte decree within 30 days after passing of the decree.

3. The learned Subordinate Judge found that the summons on the petitioner was duly served and that the application was barred by limitation and as such, he dismissed the miscellaneous case by his judgment and order dated 28.12.83.

4. The petitioner than preferred an appeal against the judgment and order before the District Judge, Jamalpur and this appeal was registered as Miscellaneous Appeal No. 8 of 1984.

5. After hearing the parties the learned District Judge agreed with the findings of the learned Subordinate Judge holding that the summons was duly served on the petitioner and that the application was barred by limitation lie then dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge by his judgment and order dated 16.9.85.

6. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order passed by the learned District Judge, Jamalpur, the petitioner approached this court in its revisional jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

7. Mr. Gour Gopal Saha, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, has argued that the records of the courts below show that the summons had been issued on the petitioner at first in the usual manner but the summons had not been served and thereafter order was passed for substituted service of the summons under Rule 20 of Order 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He also contended that after the order of substituted service was passed fresh summons had been issued for service according to Rule 20 of Order 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the summons was returned by the serving peon with a report to the effect that the summons had been duly served by beat of drum but no other particulars were given as required under Rule 20 of Order 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In this connection, Mr. Saha simply relied on the provision of Rule 20 of Order 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the report of the serving peon on the summons.

8. Mr. Abu Taher Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties, on the other hand, contended that the order recorded by the learned Subordinate Judge clearly shows that the summons had been duly served on the petitioner and as such, it is not open to this court in this revisional Jurisdiction to interfere with the finding of the courts below to the effect that the summons on the petitioner had been duly and properly served.

9. In order to resolve the question raised by the parties in this revisional application we have first of all to refer to the contents of the report at the back of the summons which is alleged to have been served on the petitioner. From the records of the learned Subordinate Judge it appears that this summons was issued from the court of the learned Subordinate Judge on the defendant vide Order No. 17 dated 6.3.79 fixing 6.4.79 as the date of return. It further appears from the record of the trial court that the summons at the first instance had been issued on the petitioner in usual course vide order No. 4 dated 4.2.78 but this summons was returned unserved on the ground that the whereabouts of the petitioner were not known (vide Order No. 6 dated 1.4.78). It also appears that on 28.5.78, on the prayer of the plaintiff- opposite party, the court again directed issuance of fresh summons for substituted service on the petitioner and others under Rule 20 of Order 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure vide order No. 8 and summons were actually issued on 21.6.78. No return of these summons was received by the court and then again on 6.3.79 vide order No. 17, after the plaintiffs prayer for issuing fresh summons, the court issued fresh summons for substituted service as provided under Rule 20 of Order 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure and Order No. 18 dated 6.4.79 shows that this time the summons was served in the substituted manner. The report of the serving peon on the body of the summons issued to the petitioner shows that he went to the locality and having failed to find the petitioner loudly announced by beat of drum, in presence of the witnesses, the contents of the summons and then sent back the summons to the issuing court stating that the summons had been duly served.

10. Mr. Saha urged that the report on the body of the summons itself shows that the requirements of Rule 20 of Order 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure were not complied with either by the court which had issued the summons or by the serving peon. Rule 20 of Order 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure runs as follows:

"20.—(1) Where the court is satisfied that there is reason to believe that the defendant is keeping out of the way for the purpose of avoiding service, or that for any other

reason the summons cannot be served in the ordinary way the Court shall order the summons to be served by affixing a copy thereof in some conspicuous place in the Court house, and also upon some conspicuous part of the house (if any) in which the defendant is known to have last resided or carried on business or personally worked for gain, or in such other manner as the Court thinks fit.

(2) Service substituted by order of the Court shall be as effectual as if it had been made on the defendant personally.

(3) Where service is substituted by order of the Court, the Court shall fix such time for the appearance of the defendant as the case may require."

<u>11. It appears from the above provision that when the court decides to effect substituted service under Rule 20 of Order 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure the court must direct that the summons be served by affixing a copy thereof in some conspicuous place in the Court-house and also upon some conspicuous part of the house in which the defendant is known to have last resided or carried on business or personally worked for gain, or in such other manner as the Court thinks fit. The mandatory provision of the above Rule is very clear. If decision is taken by the Court to effect substituted service the court must direct that a copy of the summons be affixed in the Court- house and another copy be affixed in a conspicuous part of the house of the defendant or the house in which the defendant is known to have last resided. In view of the last clause of the Rule the court was further competent to effect service by any other manner.</u>

<u>12. The intention underlying substituted service appears to be that service must be by affixing a copy of the summons at the house of the defendant and also at the court house. This is obviously for wide publicity. In addition, the rule empowers the court to effect substituted service by any other manner which the court may think fit and proper.</u>

<u>13. it appears from the report of the serving peon in the case before us that the above mandatory requirements of law were not at all complied with, and neither the order of the court nor the report of the serving peon anywhere shows that the summons was affixed at any conspicuous part of the house of the defendant or at the court house. In the above circumstances, it must be held that the courts below failed to appreciate the position of law and apply the law properly on the facts revealed in the case before them.</u>

14. It is, therefore, apparent that summons was not served on the petitioner according to the provision of Rule 20 of Order 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure and as such, the courts below committed serious error of law by holding that the summons issued for substituted service under Rule 20 of Order 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure had been duly served and by this error of law committed by the courts below they arrived at an erroneous decision refusing to allow the prayer for setting aside the ex-parte decree.

15. Mr. Abu Taher Chowdhury last of all argued that the courts below found that the petitioner's son was aware of the ex-parte decree from the very beginning and as such, the petitioner should have applied within 30 days from the date of the knowledge of her son.

16. We have already found that the summons was not served on the petitioner and the petitioner asserted in the application and also in evidence that she came to know about the ex-parte decree after obtaining the certified copy of the order thereof on 20.5.8 2.

17. A perusal of the records of the trial court shows that virtually there is no evidence to show that the fact about the ex parte decree was brought to the knowledge of the petitioner on any particular date. The date of knowledge of the son of the petitioner about the ex-parte decree, even if true, cannot be imputed on her. As such, the courts below also committed an error of law by holding that since the son of the petitioner was aware of the ex parte decree the petitioner also knew about the ex parte decree and because of this error the courts below arrived at an erroneous decision holding that the application was barred by limitation. This decision, as we have already seen, occasioned failure of justice as the petitioner could not safeguard her interests in the suit contesting it.

18. In the result, this revisional application succeeds.

19. The Rule is, accordingly, made absolute.

20. The judgment and order of the courts below are hereby set aside and the original Miscellaneous case being Miscellaneous Case No. 14 of 1982 of the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Sherpur, is allowed and the ex parte decree passed in Other Class Suit No. 33 of 1978 on 5.5.79 is set aside and the said suit is restored to its file and number.

21. In the circumstances of the case the parties are directed to bear their respective costs.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite-party Nos. 1-10 to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 12-9-2007 passed in Civil Revision No. 23 of 2005 by the Learned District Judge, Barguna allowing the Civil Revision and setting aside the judgment and order dated 16-11-2005 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Barguna Sadar, Barguna in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2004 shall not be set-aside as being illegal in as much as it was passed without properly reversing the judgment of the trial court. 
2. The facts relevant for the disposal of the Rule in short are that; 
The opposite party Nos. 1-10 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 17 of 2001 before the court of Assistant Judge, Barguna Sadar, Barguna against the petitioner along with proforma opposite party Nos. 11-72 impleading them as defendants for declaration of title and on 16-9-2003 the said title suit No. 17 of 2001 in the court of Assistant Judge, Barguna Sadar was decreed in terms of a Solenama with Opposite Party No. 46 (the defendant No. 41 in title suit No. 17 of 2001) and ex-parte against the rest. 
3. That in pursuance the petitioner on 17-2-2004 filed Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2004 under Order IX, Rule 13 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure of 1908 before the Court of Assistant Judge, Barguna Sadar against the judgment and decree dated 16-9-2003 in Title Suit No. 17 of 2001 contending inter-alia that the summons in title suit No. 17 of 2001 was not served upon the petitioner being defendant No. 43 in Title Suit No. 17 of 2001. That the opposite parties No. 1-10 being petitioners in Title Suit No. 17 of 2001 with collusion with the process server showed that the notice was served upon the petitioner, that is defendant No. 43 in the title suit and thus obtained an ex-parte judgment and decree dated 16-9-2003 and that if the Title Suit No. 17 of 2001 had not been disposed of in the absence of the petitioner, then the petitioner would have contested the suit and as such prayed that the ex-parte judgment and decree dated 6-9-2003 be set-aside being void and inoperative so that the petitioner would get a chance to contest the suit in Title Suit No. 17 of 2001 by restoring the same to its original file and number. 
4. That the opposite parties No. 1, 3 and 10 being plaintiffs in Title Suit No. 17 of 2001 contested the case denying the material allegations made against them by filing a written objection contending inter-alia that the summons of Title Suit No. 17 of 2001 was properly served upon the defendants and that the petitioner despite being fully aware of the filing of the said Title Suit abstained from contesting the suit because he was apprehensive of failure in the said suit. 
5. The Learned Senior Assistant Judge upon examination of witnesses from both sides and after hearing both parties allowed the Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2004 by his judgment and order dated 6-11-2005 and thus set-aside the earlier judgment and decree dated 16-9-2003 passed in Title Suit No. 17 of 2001 and consequently directed to restore Title Suit No. 17 of 2001 in its original file and number. 
6. Being aggrieved by order dated 16-9-2003 passed by learned Senior Assistant Judge, Barguna Sadar, Barguna the opposite parties No. 1, 3 and 10 as petitioners filed a Civil Revision being No. 23 of 2007 before the Court of District Judge, Barguna against the judgment and order dated 16-11-2005 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2004 contending inter-alia that the Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2004 was hit by the law of limitation and that they did not get a chance to cross-examine the process server since he was meanwhile transferred to another jurisdiction. 
7. The court of the District Judge upon hearing both sides vide judgment and order dated 12-9-2007 allowed the Civil Revision being No. 23 of 2007 and thereby set-aside the order dated 16-11-2005 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Barguna Sadar, Barguna in Civil Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2004. Being aggrieved by the order dated 12-9-2004 passed by the District judge dated 12-9-2007 in the Civil Revision No. 23 of 2007, the petitioners preferred instant Civil Revisional Application which is before us. 
8. Mr Tofailur Rahman with Ms Umme Salina, the learned Advocates appeared for the petitioners while no power has been filed on behalf of the opposite parties. Consequently, no one appeared on behalf of the opposite parties. 
9. Mr Tofailur Rahman submits before us that the judgment and order of the district judge was based on a misappreciation and misconception of the law and facts and thus he arrived at an erroneous finding, since the learned District Judge failed to appreciate the fact that no summons was actually served upon the petitioner. He also asserted that the District Judge over-looked certain factual matters relating to the evidence and deposition made by the witnesses. Mr. Tofailur Rahman also submits that contrary to the finding of the learned District Judge the case is not barred by the law of limitation. He also submits that there are several discrepancies in the deposition of the witnesses which was correctly taken into consideration by the court of the learned Senior Assistant Judge but which the learned District Judge over-looked particularly regarding the facts of service of summons upon the petitioner. 
10. I have heard the Learned Advocates for the petitioner and gone through the judgment and records available before me, wherefrom it transpires from the judgment of the District Judge that the Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2004 under Order IX, Rule 13 and under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure of 1908 was filed on 17-2-2004 and the petitioner of the Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2004 (Opposite Party in TS No. 17 of 2010) has admittedly stated in his petition before the court below that he had come to know about the case for the first time on 9-1-2004. Now the learned District Judge contending inter-alia on other grounds in his judgment also relied upon the ground that the Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2004 was hopelessly barred by the law of limitation. 
11. I have examined the materials on record and the relevant Article 164 of the Limitation Act, 1908, for our purpose. I have also gone through the relevant Article 164 of the Limitation Act, 1908 whereby the prescribed period of limitation for a defendant to file a suit for order to set-aside an ex-parte decree is 30 days starting from the date of the decree or, where the summons was not duly served, when the applicant has knowledge of the decree. 

12. Article 164 of the Limitation Act, 1908 reads as under;

First Schedule (contd.)-Third Division Applications (contd.)

Description of suit

Period of limitation

Time from which period begins to run.

164. By a  defendant, for an order to set aside  a decree

Passed ex-parte

 

Thirty days

 

The date of the decree or, where the summon was not duly served, when the applicant has knowledge of the decree.
13. Now in the case presently before me, it is apparent from the records that the petitioner's major contention is that in the original suit, he was a defendant, yet summons was not duly served upon him and which had therefore compelled him to file the suit under Order IX, Rule 13 and section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908. I have also perused and examined the laws and also looked into the facts surrounding the case and found that the Miscellaneous Case was filed on 17-2-2004 and the plaintiff petitioner in the Miscellaneous. Case had admittedly come to know about the said ex-parte decree for the first time on 9-1-2004. Therefore as is obvious from the records the petitioners received "knowledge" of the decree for the first time on 9-1-2004. Through my perusal of the law, the prescribed period of filing application to set-aside an ex-parte order is 'statutorily within 30 days that is the statutory time limit within date of the decree or where the summons was not duly served, the application has to be filed within 30 days of the date when the applicant has 'knowledge' of the decree. In the petitioner's case it is apparent that the prescribed 30 days to file an application ended on 9-2-2004, and, therefore, since the petitioner filed the application on 17-2-2004, it is out of time for about 9 days in filing the miscellaneous case and therefore his case falls within the mischief of Article 164 of the Limitation Act, 1908. 
14. In my view, since the suit falls under the statutory bar of the Law of Limitation provided in Article 164 of the Limitation Act, 1908, it is unnecessary and superfluous to discuss the other arguments raised in the petition particularly regarding the contention of whether the process was actually served upon the petitioner or not. The petitioners wrongly contended that the suit is not barred by the Law of Limitation, since under the circumstances it is an admitted fact that the petitioners had received knowledge of the decree on 9-1-2004 and the Civil Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2004 was filed on 17-2-2004, therefore, it was filed after the expiry of the prescribed time laid down by statute. It is regrettable under the circumstances that even assuming that there are any evidence as to the fact of the service of the summons inter-alia other evidence which could have gone in favour of the petitioner, but as to the 'statutory bar of the Law of Limitation, I cannot ignore the law and therefore it is my opinion that the District Judge has arrived at a correct decision having found that the Miscellaneous Case was hopelessly barred by limitation. 
15. This finding of mine as to the interpretation of the statutory bar of limitation under Article 164 of the Limitation Act, 1908 is supported by several other decisions of this Court, which I have also relied upon and amongst those others, I am citing one decision reported in 25 DLR 91 in the case of Most. Jahanara Begum vs Rafiqul Kader which is quoted below: 
"30 days to be counted from the date of decree or knowledge. 'Knowledge' means knowledge of decree that has been passed. 
Article 164 of Limitation Act provides a period of 30 days for filing an application for setting aside ex-parte decree. These 30 days is to be counted from the date of the decree or where the summons was not duly served, when the applicant has knowledge of the decree. 'Knowledge' is something more than mere knowledge that a decree has been passed in some Court. It is knowledge that a particular decree has been passed against him in a particular Court in favour of a particular person for a particular sum (or in respect of particular property) and not merely the knowledge that a decree has been passed by some Court against him, Mst. Johara Begum vs Rafiqul Kader 25 DLR 91." 
16. From a perusal of the decision quoted above and in view of my finding in this case it is clear that the suit is, in limine, barred by the law of limitation therefore, I deliberately refrain from entering in to the merits of the case, since, as I have observed above it would be an useless and superfluous exercise on my part. 
17. In the light of the facts and circumstances as stated above and the relevant law relied upon, I find no merit in the Rule and it is therefore liable to be discharged. 
18. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any Order as to costs and the judgment and order dated 12-9-2007 passed by the District Judge is hereby affirmed. 
The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated. 
End.
